title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: Apparel remained protected as other tariffs fell
text:
Apparel remained protected as other tariffs fell




Lewis Hine, 1908 · Library of Congress, public domain.


After the Tokyo Round, 1979
6.5% average U.S. tariff on manufactured goods.
22.5% average U.S. tariff on apparel.
What explains this difference?


Trade agreements change the cost of crossing a border.


Rivoli, “Dogs Snarling Together”; historical averages reported in the assigned chapter.


Timing: 0–5 minutes.
Introduce the fourth Module 3 border cost: trade rules. The photograph shows the earlier mill economy, not conditions in 1979. Tariff averages are the historical figures reported by Rivoli, citing Cline. Do not mix them with the Kennedy Round.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: Your IB Voice
text:
Your IB Voice


Question


What was the political logic behind the Multifiber Arrangement? Whose problem did it solve, and what did each side give up?



10 minutes · Individual · Notes permitted · No internet or LLMs


Timing: 5–15 minutes.
Expect three kinds of answer: the president’s problem (Nixon’s 1968 promise to Thurmond and the Southern vote), the industry’s problem (cotton quotas pushed imports into wool and synthetics), and the trade agenda’s problem (textiles had to be paid to step aside from liberalization). All three are in Rivoli and all three are correct; do not present them as rivals. Students may not yet have Irwin’s vocabulary for them.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: Explanations
text:
Explanations

Whose problem did the Multifiber Arrangement solve?


Who won and who lost?


Timing: 15–20 minutes.
Take three brief responses. Write each on the board as a problem, a fixer, and a payer (for example: Nixon needed Southern votes; Thurmond could deliver them; apparel buyers paid). Preserve the board for the closing revision. Do not yet name geography or collective action; the next section supplies those.

section: Three objectives shaped U.S. tariff policy
text:
Three objectives shaped U.S. tariff policy







Product
Tariff
Import value




A
5%
$500,000

12%

$300,000



Weighted average: (5% × $500,000 + 12% × $200,000 + 0% × $300,000) ÷ $1,000,000 = 4.9%.
Import value equals price × quantity. Holding quantities fixed, a higher price for Product B gives the 12% tariff more weight and raises the average. The total imports tariff includes Product C at 0%. The dutiable-import average excludes Product C.


Revenue: 1790–1860
Duties financed the federal government.
Restriction: 1860–1934
Protection supported domestic producers.
Reciprocity: from 1934
Negotiated cuts opened foreign markets.


The Civil War and then the Great Depression changed the objective.


Irwin, Introduction, pp. 2–8, Figure I.1 (original figure, cropped from p. 6).


Timing: 20–24 minutes.
Irwin traces the history through 2015. The eras describe dominant objectives, not constant rates.
Explain the weighted average with three products. Product A faces a 5 percent tariff and has an import value of $500,000. Product B faces a 12 percent tariff and has an import value of $200,000. Product C enters duty-free and has an import value of $300,000.
Multiply each tariff rate by its import value: $25,000 for Product A, $24,000 for Product B, and zero for Product C. The sum is $49,000. Divide by total import value of $1 million to obtain the 4.9 percent weighted average. The simple average of 5, 12, and 0 percent would be 5.67 percent, but that calculation gives each product equal weight.
Import prices affect the weights because import value equals price multiplied by quantity. Holding quantities constant, a rise in Product B’s price increases its share of import value. The 12 percent tariff then receives more weight, pulling the average upward. A rise in Product C’s price would increase the weight on the zero tariff and pull the average downward.
For the total-import series, the weights cover all imports and duty-free goods have a tariff rate of zero. For the dutiable-import series, the weights cover only goods subject to a tariff. Do not extend the historical endpoint into a claim about 2026.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: Regional interests persisted in congressional votes
text:
Regional interests persisted in congressional votes


Tariff vote, 1828


Tariff vote, 1929



Exporting regions sought market access. Import-competing regions sought protection. Congress (institution) translates these interests into tariff policy.


Irwin, Introduction, pp. 10–16, Figure I.5; maps by Citrin GIS/Applied Spatial Analysis Lab, Dartmouth College. Cropped from p. 16.


Timing: 24–27 minutes.
Ask students to identify the persistent regional pattern before explaining it. These are votes on the 1828 and 1929 bills, not identical districts or identical tariff schedules. The 1929 vote preceded enactment of the 1930 tariff. Irwin reports a 0.70 correlation across state delegations. Omit the extra NAFTA correlation to keep the map central.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: A general model of trade policy
text:
A general model of trade policy



Regional economic interests
Exporters seek market access. Import-competing producers seek protection.


→



Political institutions
Institutions filter competing demands. Electoral rules shape representation. Trade authority determines who decides.


→



Trade policy
Governments set tariffs and quotas. They also negotiate trade agreements.


Political institutions filter regional interests, so similar interests can produce different trade policies across countries.


Raniel Jose Castaneda, rice terraces, Philippines, CC BY-SA 4.0; European Parliament, CC0; William Cho, Port of Singapore, CC BY-SA 2.0.


Timing: set by instructor.
Present this as a general model that can travel across countries. Economic geography creates regional interests because production and employment are concentrated in particular places. Political institutions filter those demands. Electoral systems determine how regions gain representation, while constitutions and statutes assign trade authority to legislatures, executives, or both. The result may be a tariff, quota, subsidy, or negotiated agreement. Ask students how the same regional divide might produce a different outcome under proportional representation, a presidential system, or a highly centralized state.
The photographs make the model international rather than presenting the U.S. case as universal. They illustrate production in the Philippines, representation in the European Union, and cross-border commerce in Singapore. They are visual examples, not evidence of a single causal case.
[Sources] - Douglas A. Irwin, Clashing over Commerce (2017), Introduction, pp. 3 and 13-15. Regional economic interests and U.S. tariff politics. - Helen V. Milner, Interests, Institutions, and Information (1997), chapter 1. Domestic interests filtered through political institutions. - Image credits and licenses appear on the slide.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: Concentrated gains > diffuse costs
text:
Concentrated gains > diffuse costs




Protected producers
A tariff can concentrate jobs and profits in a few firms and districts. Each firm has a strong reason to organize.
Consumers and retailers
The added cost spreads across many purchases. Each buyer has less reason to lobby. Retailers gained influence after organizing in the 1980s.


Political strength follows the incentive and capacity to organize.


James Madison Wikimedia Commons.


Timing: set by instructor.
Madison opens Irwin with conflicting manufacturing and landed interests. Use the tariff example to explain the collective-action problem. Producers may receive large benefits concentrated in a few firms and places, giving them a strong reason to organize. Consumers each pay a small amount across many purchases, weakening the incentive for any one buyer to lobby.
Give the T-shirt version: a few cents on every shirt for millions of buyers against jobs and profits concentrated in one town. Retailers eventually overcame their coordination problem by forming RITAC to counter the textile coalition. Exporters and downstream producers can also organize for liberalization.
[Sources] - Douglas A. Irwin, Clashing over Commerce (2017), Introduction, pp. 1-2 and 18-20. - Pietra Rivoli, “Dogs Snarling Together,” pp. 1-2 and 12. Retailers and RITAC. - Mancur Olson, The Logic of Collective Action (1965). General collective-action mechanism; not assigned.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: 1934: Congress delegated tariff negotiation to Executive
text:
1934: Congress delegated tariff negotiation to Executive




A different procedure
The president could cut tariffs by up to half in exchange for foreign cuts.
Agreements took effect by presidential proclamation, with no vote on each one.
A different objective
Cordell Hull linked reciprocal trade liberalization to peace and international cooperation.


The Depression shifted political power. Hull supplied an alternative policy and a reason to pursue it.


Irwin, Introduction, pp. 21–27; U.S. Tariff Commission, historical account, p. 1; USTR photograph.


Timing: 27–31 minutes.
Distinguish congressional delegation and renewal of authority from later congressional votes on implementing legislation. The RTAA did not require subsequent approval of each agreement: the president proclaimed the new rates, and Congress voted only when the three-year authority came up for renewal. Say aloud that the slide describes 1934. Since the Trade Act of 1974, agreements that change U.S. law return to Congress for a single up-or-down vote on implementing legislation with no amendments, the procedure now called Trade Promotion Authority; that is how NAFTA, the Uruguay Round agreements, and CAFTA-DR were approved, and it is what Irwin means on p. 21 when he says Congress has had to approve each agreement since the 1970s. Irwin’s stronger claim (p. 26) is that the RTAA is the one regime change with no compelling interest-group explanation: it was tied to a shift in ideas after Hawley-Smoot, and Hull carried it. Photograph: USTR, public domain.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: The Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act
text:
The Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act



01

Congress set tariffs
Congress wrote product-specific rates. Members bargained for industries in their districts.


02

Pressure for change
The Depression and foreign retaliation exposed the costs of high tariffs.


03

Congress delegated
The RTAA authorized the president for three years. Tariff reductions were capped at 50%.


04

The president negotiated
Reciprocal agreements took effect without a new congressional vote on each deal.


Outcome by 1946: Agreements with 27 countries affected nearly 2,000 U.S. products and provided a model for GATT.


U.S. International Trade Commission, History of U.S. Trade Policy Since 1934, pp. 73-75; USITC, Reversing Protectionism, pp. 4-6.


Start with the institutional baseline. The Constitution assigns tariff authority to Congress, and Congress traditionally revised the tariff schedule through legislation. Product-specific bargaining encouraged members to trade votes for duties protecting industries in their districts.
Explain why Congress changed the procedure. The Depression, the international reaction to Smoot-Hawley, and the collapse of U.S. exports strengthened the case for lower barriers. Foreign governments had little reason to lower their tariffs unless the United States offered concessions in return. Roosevelt and Hull argued that the president needed authority to negotiate that exchange across products and countries.
Congress retained control over the statute. It initially authorized the president for three years and capped tariff reductions at 50 percent of existing rates. The executive could conclude an agreement and proclaim the resulting rates without returning to Congress for a vote on each deal.
State the outcome. From 1934 through 1946, 27 countries signed bilateral agreements with the United States. The agreements affected nearly 2,000 U.S. products, about half the products subject to duties in 1930. This bilateral program supplied a model for the GATT negotiations in 1947.
Keep one qualification for the next section: the negotiations were bilateral, while U.S. tariff concessions generally extended to other countries under most-favored-nation treatment. The following MFN slide explains that rule.
If asked whether this is still the procedure: no. Proclamation without a vote worked while agreements only changed tariff rates. Once agreements began to require changes in U.S. law (after the Kennedy Round), Congress adopted fast track in the Trade Act of 1974: negotiating authority is still granted in advance, but the implementing legislation gets a single up-or-down vote with no amendments.
[Sources] - Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act of 1934, Pub. L. No. 73-316. - U.S. International Trade Commission, History of U.S. Trade Policy Since 1934 (2010), pp. 73-75, https://www.usitc.gov/publications/332/us_trade_policy_since1934_ir6_pub4094.pdf. - Peter Herman and Michael Ferrantino, Reversing Protectionism: A First Look at Product-level Trade Data from Smoot-Hawley to the GATT (USITC, 2024), pp. 4-6, https://www.usitc.gov/publications/332/working_papers/2024-12-a_reversing_protectionism.pdf. - Douglas A. Irwin, Clashing over Commerce (2017), Introduction, pp. 21-27.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: MFN: a tariff cut for one member is a tariff cut for all
text:
MFN: a tariff cut for one member is a tariff cut for all
Countries A, B, C, and D are all GATT/WTO members. A cuts its shirt tariff from 10% to 5% in exchange for a cut by B on A’s exports.


GATT Article I: Country A cannot favor one member over another. C and D get the 5% rate without giving anything in return.


GATT, Article I. Hypothetical countries and rates; photograph on preceding divider: WTO, GATT signing, 1947.


Timing: 34–39 minutes.
Define most-favored-nation treatment aloud: under GATT Article I, an importing country applies the same tariff to like products from every member, so any advantage granted to one must be granted to all. Membership does not set a country’s tariffs; it caps them at the rates the country has bound. Lowering them takes a negotiating round.
Walk the diagram. A charged 10 percent on shirts from B, C, and D. A and B strike a bargain and A cuts to 5 percent. Article I means shirts from C and D enter at 5 percent too, though neither gave A anything on shirts. A collects the tariff when the shirts enter.
If a student asks why anyone gives a concession that everyone receives: reciprocity is secured by the round, not by each cut. In the first five rounds (1947–1961) each tariff was negotiated item by item between the importer and its principal supplier, the country that gained most from the cut and so would pay most for it, and the round then added up the pairs. From the Kennedy Round (1964–67) members instead cut across the board by a common formula and negotiated lists of exceptions. Under either method a member that gets A’s shirt rate for nothing is paying elsewhere in the round through its own concessions. The members that were exempted from paying were the developing countries, which is why the Uruguay Round insisted they contribute for the first time, and why the MFA came onto the table.
Draw out the political consequence: a country cannot make a concession to one partner without making it to all, so postwar tariff cutting had to be multilateral. “Like products” matters. MFN has permitted exceptions; the next slide introduces the one for free trade areas.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: A free trade agreement keeps the cut from non-members
text:
A free trade agreement keeps the cut from non-members
A and B form a free trade area. Shirts from B now enter A at 0%. Shirts from C and D still pay the 5% MFN rate.


GATT Article XXIV allows this exception to MFN. It works only if A can tell a shirt made in B from a shirt that passed through B.


GATT, Articles I and XXIV. Hypothetical countries and rates.


Timing: 39–44 minutes.
Define a tariff preference aloud: a lower tariff for an agreement partner than the MFN tariff applied to other members. Begin from the previous slide’s diagram, with A charging 5 percent on shirts from B, C, and D. A and B then form a free trade area, and A eliminates the tariff on shirts that qualify under the agreement. B pays 0 percent; C and D remain outside and still pay 5 percent. GATT Article XXIV permits free trade areas and customs unions under defined conditions, including that they cover substantially all trade. This is the exception to the MFN rule on the previous slide.
Ask the class why C does not simply ship its shirts through B. That is the problem rules of origin solve, and it is the question the rules-of-origin activity takes up. Do not answer it here.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: Textile protection supported broader trade bargains
text:
Textile protection supported broader trade bargains




Kennedy, 1961–62
Cotton quotas helped secure textile-industry support for broader trade liberalization.
Reagan, 1980
He promised to limit import growth to growth in the domestic market. Existing agreements made that promise impossible to fulfill.


Southern concentration helped the industry organize. Unfulfilled promises also generated pressure for stronger protection.


Rivoli, “Dogs Snarling Together”, especially the presidential promises and textile coalition. Background photograph on preceding divider: Lewis Hine, North Carolina, 1908, Library of Congress.


Timing: 44–47 minutes.
Explain Rivoli’s congressional geography: firms, workers, and regional representatives shared stakes. Her reported 60 percent concentration is a historical claim, not a current estimate. Kennedy delivered quota arrangements; Reagan’s roughly 1 percent promise conflicted with roughly 6 percent growth in existing agreements. The later Jenkins bill belongs to the resulting pressure, not evidence that every promise was kept.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: Quotas redirected imports across places and products
text:
Quotas redirected imports across places and products




Museum exhibit, 2008 · InSapphoWeTrust, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.


Japan quota → Hong Kong
U.S. cotton-goods imports from Hong Kong rose nearly 700%, 1956–61.
Cotton quotas → other fibers
U.S. synthetic-fiber imports from developing countries rose 2,500%, 1964–70.


The Multifiber Arrangement (MFA), 1974, extended quotas to more countries and fibers as producers changed sourcing routes.


Rivoli, “Dogs Snarling Together”, discussion of the Eisenhower-era Japanese restraint (Rivoli does not date it; 1957 is external), cotton arrangements, and the MFA.


Timing: 47–50 minutes.
The photograph is a museum reconstruction, not an original 1960s factory photograph. The percentages describe the flows and periods reported by Rivoli; they are not estimates of the quota’s causal effect. The 1974 Multifiber Arrangement widened the regime beyond cotton. Ask which input or location a firm would change when one route is capped.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: Global sourcing divided the textile coalition
text:
Global sourcing divided the textile coalition


Retailers organized for easier imports. Developing-country exporters sought an end to the MFA in exchange for concessions in services and intellectual property.


Rivoli, “Dogs Snarling Together”, discussion of retailer organization, upstream conflicts, and the International Textiles and Clothing Bureau.


Timing: 50–53 minutes.
Distinguish two changes: apparel firms and retailers organized around access to foreign inputs and products; developing-country exporters coordinated international bargaining. Fabric mills could favor cheaper foreign yarn even as spinners sought restrictions. A coalition split alone did not mechanically end protection.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: The textile coalition could no longer overcome a veto
text:
The textile coalition could no longer overcome a veto

The 1985 Jenkins bill had 230 cosponsors and would have imposed stronger global textile quotas.

Protection still commanded a large House majority. The coalition fell eight votes short of overriding President Reagan’s veto.


Rivoli, “Dogs Snarling Together”, Jenkins bill and override discussion.


Timing: 53–56 minutes.
Present this vote as a limit on coalition power, not an abrupt disappearance of support. The bill had 230 cosponsors. The House later voted 276 to 149 to override Reagan’s veto, eight votes short of the required two-thirds majority.
The large majority shows that textile protection remained politically powerful. The failed override shows that the coalition could no longer force an expansion of quotas over presidential opposition. This failure belongs between the domestic coalition split and the Uruguay Round bargain that produced the ATC.
The bill and veto occurred in 1985; the failed override vote occurred on August 6, 1986. Rivoli gives the 276 votes and the eight-vote margin. The 149 opposing votes and the date come from the House roll-call record.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: The end of textile quotas, 1995–2005
text:
The end of textile quotas, 1995–2005


1995
The agreement begins
The Agreement on Textiles and Clothing (ATC) gives governments ten years to eliminate the Multifiber Arrangement quotas.

1995–2004
Governments delay sensitive products
Early targets count products that already face no quota. About 85% of actual quotas remain at the end of 2004.

2005
The deadline arrives
The remaining MFA quotas end. Tariffs and other trade rules continue.


The ATC ended quotas on a schedule, while governments postponed politically sensitive products until the deadline.


Rivoli, “Dogs Snarling Together”; WTO, Agreement on Textiles and Clothing.


Timing: 53–56 minutes.
Explain the formal schedule only after the story is clear. The ATC required 16 percent of the 1990 import-volume base to enter normal WTO rules in 1995, another 17 percent in 1998, another 18 percent in 2002, and the remaining 49 percent in 2005.
Those percentages measured import volume covered by product categories, not the number of active quotas removed. Governments could count products that already faced no quota toward the early targets. Rivoli’s examples include parachutes, kelims, silk sport bags, and laparoscopy sponges.
Rivoli reports that about 85 percent of quotas remained at the end of 2004. Most binding quotas therefore disappeared in the final stage. The ATC ended the quota regime in 2005, while tariffs and other trade rules continued.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: The New MFA Logic
text:
The New MFA Logic
For forty years, presidents gave the textile industry quotas so that U.S. trade liberalization of other sectors could proceed.

In the Uruguay Round the United States gave up the MFA so that developing countries would accept liberalization of U.S. services and intellectual property.


Rivoli, “Dogs Snarling Together”, the Uruguay Round and the ITCB.


Timing: set by instructor.
Rivoli’s phrase: America “would now have to pay the developing countries to move out of the way of broader trade liberalization.” Connect to the board: the problem changed (the United States wanted services and IP rules), the fixer changed (the ITCB), and the payer changed (the domestic textile coalition, already split). The mechanisms from Irwin did not change; the geography of who was concentrated did.
[Sources] Rivoli, pp. 13–14.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: Should sewing in Honduras make the shirt regional?
text:
Should sewing in Honduras make the shirt regional?
A rule of origin says which production steps must happen inside the region for the finished garment to enter the United States duty-free.

Inside the region means the United States, five Central American countries, and the Dominican Republic.

The fabric comes from outside CAFTA-DR. Honduras cuts and sews the shirt. Should that be enough for duty-free entry?


U.S. Department of Commerce, CAFTA-DR textiles. Historical teaching example; product-specific rules and exceptions apply.


Timing: 56–58 minutes.
Historical, simplified example based on CAFTA-DR at implementation. The agreement was signed in 2004; Congress approved implementing legislation in 2005; it entered into force for Honduras in April 2006. Avoid undated claims about present-day all-in tariffs.
Make the two definitions explicit before the activity. First, the rule governs only the tariff on the finished garment when it enters the United States; a Honduran plant or U.S. mill that imports Asian fabric or yarn still pays whatever tariff applies to that input. Second, the members are the United States, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, and the Dominican Republic. The candidate rules students will propose, from strictest to loosest, are cotton-forward (all four stages inside), yarn-forward (yarn, fabric, and sewing inside; cotton from anywhere), fabric-forward (fabric and sewing inside; yarn and cotton from anywhere), and sewing-only. Do not list these on the slide; let the roles produce them. Ask whether sewing alone should be sufficient. Hold the actual rule until after reports.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: Negotiate a rule of origin
text:
Negotiate a rule of origin

You will be assigned one industry role.



1. U.S. yarn spinner


2. U.S. fabric mill


3. Honduran sewing plant


4. U.S. apparel brand


5. Asian fabric mill


6. U.S. retailer



Production stages: Cotton grown → Yarn spun → Fabric knit → Garment sewn


Advocate: Which stages should the agreement require within CAFTA-DR?
Explain: How does your rule affect your business?


5-10 minutes · One rule


Timing: 58–69 minutes.
58–59: students form groups with three or four people seated near them. Distribute one role card to each group, with repeated roles as needed. 59–69: ten minutes of work. Tell groups that they are proposing what the agreement should require, not guessing the existing rule. Their report should name a required starting stage and explain one effect on their business. No internet research is needed.
Expected answers. Each producer proposes the rule that begins at its own stage. Spinner: yarn-forward, and not cotton-forward, because cotton is its input. Fabric mill: fabric-forward, so its fabric is required but it may buy foreign yarn; this is the spinner-versus-mill split from Rivoli. Honduran sewing plant: sewing-only by cost, but the stronger answer is that it accepts yarn-forward because the agreement cannot pass Congress without the spinners and mills. Apparel brand: sewing-only, so Asian fabric sewn in Honduras qualifies. Asian fabric mill: sewing-only, the only rule under which its fabric can be in a qualifying garment. Retailer: sewing-only, but close to indifferent, since it can already import finished Asian garments and pay the tariff.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: CAFTA-DR generally uses a yarn-forward rule
text:
CAFTA-DR generally uses a yarn-forward rule



What qualifies
Yarn spinning, fabric production, and garment assembly occur within CAFTA-DR. Cotton may come from outside the region.

The exception
Garments containing yarns or fabrics on the short-supply list still qualify, even though those inputs are made outside the region.


Only garments made from regional yarn and fabric qualify, which is what creates demand for both. The short-supply list lets a garment qualify with listed foreign inputs.


U.S. Department of Commerce, CAFTA-DR textiles. See the general yarn-forward rule and commercial-availability exceptions.


Timing: 69–77 minutes.
69–73: take four selected reports at 45 seconds each, leaving one minute for transitions and comparison. Include a spinner, mill, apparel/sewing, and retailer/exporter perspective. 73–77: reveal this slide and debrief. Four of the six roles wanted a looser rule than yarn-forward; the two that did not are concentrated in Southern districts. Ask which roles wanted a different rule, then ask which of them had a senator. The short-supply list is how the others were bought off. Yarn-forward is a simplified description of the garment rule; specific product and component rules apply. Cotton growers may benefit indirectly, but regional cotton is not required here. Retailers did not get nothing. Separate the fabric mill’s desire for foreign yarn from the spinner’s interest. If time permits, invite one sentence connecting this conflict to a team’s own industry. Do not add a new research task.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: Three levels of regional integration
text:
Three levels of regional integration



Free trade area
Example: USMCA
A Mexican-built car needs proof that it meets USMCA origin rules. The three members can set different tariffs on cars from Japan.


Customs union
Example: Southern African Customs Union
Five Southern African countries apply a common external tariff. Goods produced within SACU move among members without customs duties.


Single market
Example: European Union
Goods, services, capital, and people move under shared rules. A French firm can hire an Italian citizen without a work permit.


Deeper integration removes more border barriers and constrains more national policy choices. The euro area adds a shared currency.


USTR: USMCA rules of origin; SACU: common external tariff; European Commission: single market. Images: U.S. Treasury, public domain; SACU map by Htonl, public domain; EU flags by Fred Romero, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.


Timing: 77–81 minutes.
Start with the firm-level examples. Under USMCA, the members remove tariffs only for qualifying goods and retain separate external tariffs. A firm therefore documents origin and may face a different tariff depending on which member imports the product.
SACU illustrates the next level. Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, and South Africa form one customs territory with a common external tariff. Goods produced within SACU move among members free of customs duties. The members also share customs and excise revenue through a common revenue pool.
The single market goes further by supporting the free movement of goods, services, capital, and people under common rules. National and sectoral barriers remain. The euro area adds a shared currency and has different membership from the single market. Do not imply that the single market harmonizes all corporate taxes.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: Reflection: return to your IB Voice
text:
Reflection: return to your IB Voice

Does the logic that created the MFA also explain how it ended?


Timing: 84–88 minutes.
Allow three minutes to write and one minute for a response. Strong revisions keep the same mechanism (someone with leverage is paid to step aside) and show that the parties changed: apparel firms and retailers organized, spinners and mills split, and developing countries bargained as a bloc. Weak revisions treat the MFA’s end as a change of heart. Preserve ideas and institutions; do not collapse both readings into one deterministic mechanism.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: Monday: private enforcement in the diamond trade
text:
Monday: private enforcement in the diamond trade





Why might firms rely on private rules to enforce a trading agreement?


Bernstein examines reputation and dispute resolution in the diamond trade.



Photograph: Wikimedia Commons, CC0.


Timing: 88–90 minutes.
One-minute preview and one-minute buffer. Connect rules governing market access to rules governing exchange. Private enforcement does not mean an absence of state law.

title: How Trade Agreements Organize Markets
section: Module 3 summary and beyond
text:
Module 3 summary and beyond

Borders divide business among different currencies, laws, tax systems, and trade rules.
Those differences determine which cross-border activities are feasible, profitable, and risky.
Firms respond through choices about sourcing, financing, ownership, legal structure, and political engagement.
Those choices distribute gains and losses, create dependencies, and shape how shocks travel.
The rest of the course examines how firms organize around these constraints and how (and why) firms and governments try to change them.


Timing: set by instructor.
Place Module 3 in the arc of the syllabus. Module 1 mapped the system behind a global product. Module 2 explained why trade creates value and political conflict. Module 3 established the external environment in which firms operate: transport systems, currencies, legal jurisdictions, taxes, and trade rules. Module 4 now asks how firms choose ownership, contracts, locations, and coordination mechanisms within that environment. Later modules examine the dependencies those choices create, the bargaining power they confer, and the way shocks and political change move through the system.
The four Module 3 cases provide evidence for this synthesis. Containers changed the feasible geography of production. Thailand shows how financing choices allocate currency risk. Apple shows how a firm uses multiple legal entities across jurisdictions. Trade agreements show how political bargains structure access to markets. The final bullet is the bridge to the remainder of the course.
[Sources] 2026-09-08 containers deck (freight at 12 percent of export value against a 7 percent tariff; five costs; the decade of standards and bargains). 2026-09-09 currency-crisis deck (25 to 56 baht per dollar; mismatch of revenue, costs, and debt). 2026-09-14 legal-jurisdictions deck (Braeburn Capital; transfer price at $80 versus $70; royalties; EU state-aid recovery). This deck (MFN, rules of origin, the MFA bargain).

title: Exchange Rates and Currency Crises
section: Thai Baht Collapse of 1997-1998
text:
Thai Baht Collapse of 1997-1998


FRED DEXTHUS, Board of Governors H.10 daily noon buying rates


A Thai factory in 1996: baht wages, dollar loans, a fixed exchange rate.
The baht then moved from about 25 per dollar to more than 50 within six months, turning dollar debt into a firm-level crisis.


Timing: 0-3. Start with the graph. The point is the scale and speed of devaluation. Students should see that a firm’s loan balance can change before the firm changes operations.
Source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Thai Baht to U.S. Dollar Spot Exchange Rate [DEXTHUS], retrieved from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Daily noon buying rates in New York for cable transfers payable in foreign currencies.

section: Your IB Voice
text:
Your IB Voice


Question


At what point could an actor in Blustein’s account have changed the course of Thailand’s crisis? Identify the actor, the action they could have taken, and why they failed to take it.



10 minutes · Individual · Notes permitted · No internet or LLMs


Commit to an answer before we reconstruct the sequence.


Diagnoses onto the board. Push on what each actor knew and when: firms knew the rate was fixed but not that reserves were committed; lenders knew the interest gap; the central bank knew the reserves; the IMF knew short-term debt was high. Return to this board at the end.

section: Supply and demand set a floating exchange rate
text:
Supply and demand set a floating exchange rate



Demand for dollars
Japanese buyers exchange yen for dollars to purchase US goods and assets.

Supply of dollars
Americans exchange dollars for yen to purchase Japanese goods and assets.


The nominal exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. More yen per dollar means dollar appreciation and yen depreciation.


Timing: 6-9. The vertical axis quotes the price of one dollar in yen. A rise in yen per dollar means the dollar appreciates and the yen depreciates. The quantity axis measures dollars traded per period.
Demand for dollars rises when Japanese purchases of US goods or assets increase. Supply of dollars rises when Americans purchase more Japanese goods or assets.

title: Exchange Rates and Currency Crises
section: The IMF lends when a country cannot meet its external payments
text:
The IMF lends when a country cannot meet its external payments



Temporary financing goes to member governments facing external-payment problems.
The government and IMF negotiate policy conditions intended to restore reserves and access to financing.
The IMF does not rescue individual firms or repay their private loans.


The central dispute concerns the conditions attached to IMF financing.




IMF headquarters · Ajay Suresh / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0



Timing: 6-9. Enough background to allocate responsibility later. The Fund lends to governments, not firms, and does not repay private creditors.

title: Exchange Rates and Currency Crises
section: A fixed rate made dollar debt look safe
text:
A fixed rate made dollar debt look safe



25


baht per dollar, held for more than a decade


Every morning the Bank of Thailand set the rate and bought or sold dollars to maintain it.
Japanese carmakers and Thai exporters planned around it.


A fixed rate removes the exchange-rate calculation from every decision. This reduces investment risk, as long as the rate is credible.


Timing: 22-26. Rate set each morning on a formula with small weights on the yen and mark, unlimited dollars at the rate plus or minus 0.02 baht. Growth above 9 percent a year from 1986; exports up 19 percent a year in the early 1990s.

title: Exchange Rates and Currency Crises
section: Dollar borrowing created a currency mismatch
text:
Dollar borrowing created a currency mismatch
$56 billion was borrowed through the Bangkok International Banking Facilities by 1997, three times the 1994 level.
The facility, launched in 1992 with IMF support, made foreign-currency borrowing cheaper.


Borrowers and lenders treated the peg as protection.


Timing: 26-30. BIBFs were meant to borrow abroad and relend abroad; most was lent inside Thailand and converted to baht. Inflows reached 13 percent of GDP in 1995, mostly short term. Finance One borrowed about $600 million abroad.

title: Exchange Rates and Currency Crises
section: Cheap foreign money flowed into property and stocks
text:
Cheap foreign money flowed into property and stocks


Credit to Thailand’s private sector: $89 billion in 1992, $204 billion in 1996.
Bangkok office space added in 1996: 600,000 square metres, half empty.
Official bad-loan rate by May 1997: 12 percent.

The assets earned baht. The debts were owed in dollars.




Sathorn Unique Tower · Chainwit. / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0



Timing: 30-34. Finance companies were a fifth of all credit. Muang Thong Thani was a billion-dollar estate with weeds in unsold buildings. The central bank knew in 1993 that nearly 40 percent of Bangkok Bank of Commerce assets were nonperforming and did not act.

title: Exchange Rates and Currency Crises
section: As the dollar rose, Thai exports became less competitive
text:
As the dollar rose, Thai exports became less competitive

Pegged to a rising dollar from 1995, Thai clothes, shoes, and electronics became more expensive on world markets. Export growth in 1996: flat.



A fixed rate imports the movements of the currency it is fixed to.


Timing: 34-37. Current account = earnings from abroad minus payments abroad. Thailand 1996: −8% of GDP, financed by short-term dollar loans on roughly 90-day terms. Ask why a deficit is not by itself a crisis, and what changes when foreign lending stops.

title: Exchange Rates and Currency Crises
section: The warnings came before the reserves ran out
text:
The warnings came before the reserves ran out

IMF warnings: a January letter, visits in March and May, and advice to adjust the rate and widen the band.
The refusal. Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi, deputy governor of Bank of Thailand, argued that Mexico had tried a controlled devaluation and failed. If 25 will not hold, why would 28, or 30?

The Bank of Thailand held the peg, but its ability to defend it disappeared.


Timing: 37-41. Short-selling from January, including Soros’s Quantum Fund. Camdessus letter 31 January; missions in March and May.

section: The reserve headline concealed the cost of defense
text:
The reserve headline concealed the cost of defense

Thai ministers who asked for the number were refused by their own central bank. Fischer was given it in late July, on condition that he tell no one else at the Fund.

The reported reserve figure did not show how much cash remained available.


Timing: 41-45. $38 billion in early 1997. $10 billion spent on 14 May alone. $23 billion committed forward by late May. About $2 billion usable by June. These are checkpoints, not a subtraction.

title: Exchange Rates and Currency Crises

text:
Capital controls interrupted short-selling while dollar demand continued



Hedge fund
Borrow baht → sell baht → borrowing blocked
Attack interrupted

Thai borrower
Dollar debt due → sell baht for dollars → repay loan
Pressure continued


Domestic dollar demand kept pressure on the baht.


Timing: 45-50. 15 May: the 29 banks in Thailand barred from lending baht offshore. Hedge-fund losses $400 to $500 million; overnight baht rates above 1,000 percent. Amnuay resigned 19 June and the domestic run began.

title: Exchange Rates and Currency Crises
section: The baht cost of dollar debt more than doubled
text:
The baht cost of dollar debt more than doubled


A $1 million loan went from 25 million to 56 million baht. Revenue in baht did not move.


Timing: 50-54. 25 before the 2 July float, 32 on 25 July, 56 in early 1998. Ask who is helped: an exporter with dollar revenue and baht costs gains. Selected milestones, not a daily series.

Rerun the year for one Thai firm



Annual cash flow

At 25, 32, and 56 baht per dollar, calculate:

Operating profit before debt repayment
The baht value of the $20 million principal
Cash remaining after repaying the principal

Could the firm repay the loan from this year’s operations? What risk remains if the loan must be renewed?


12 minutes · Teams · One sheet per team


Timing: 59-75. Give teams 12 minutes, then confirm the calculations and discuss why the firm depends on refinancing even before the devaluation. Numbers are stylized, not Blustein’s. Treat the listed exchange rate as the rate applied to all dollar cash flows in each scenario.
Operating profit in millions of baht = 700 + (12 × rate) − (16 × rate) − 250 = 450 − (4 × rate).
At 25: operating profit = 350. Principal repayment = 500. Cash after principal = −150. At 32: operating profit = 322. Principal repayment = 640. Cash after principal = −318. At 56: operating profit = 226. Principal repayment = 1,120. Cash after principal = −894.
The firm cannot repay the principal from this year’s operations even at 25 baht per dollar. It therefore depends on existing cash, new financing, or renewal of the loan. The devaluation increases its net dollar burden because imports exceed export revenue and the principal remains due in dollars.
If the loan must be renewed, the firm faces rollover risk. The lender may refuse to renew or demand worse terms.

title: Exchange Rates and Currency Crises
section: The rescue demanded austerity from a collapsing economy
text:
The rescue demanded austerity from a collapsing economy



−10%


Thai GDP in 1998; unemployment tripled, urban wages fell 8 percent


Thailand first sought bilateral help from Japan and China. Both declined to act outside an IMF-led program.
The $17.2 billion package later included contributions from both. The United States contributed no funds.
The IMF required fiscal measures equal to 3 percent of GDP.


The current account moved from a deficit of nearly 8 percent of GDP in 1996 to a surplus of nearly 13 percent in 1998 as collapsing domestic demand crushed imports.


Timing: 75-80. Keep the IMF debate short. Disclosure of the $23 billion, forced by the US Treasury as a loan condition, sent the baht to a new low the day after approval. section: The same devaluation, different firms
text:
The same devaluation, different firms


Exporter
Dollar revenue
Baht costs
The dollar buys more baht.
The firm’s position improves.

Domestic borrower
Baht revenue
Dollar debt
The debt costs more baht to repay.
The firm’s position deteriorates.


Exchange-rate risk comes from a mismatch among a firm’s revenue, costs, and debt. A forward can lock in the rate for a known dollar payment. Loan renewal remains a separate risk.


Timing: 80-84. The same baht devaluation helps a firm with dollar revenue and baht costs, while it harms a firm with baht revenue and dollar debt. Define exposure as the firm’s position in a currency. Define mismatch as revenue, costs, and debt being denominated in different currencies. Define a hedge or forward as a contract that locks in an exchange rate for a known future payment. Distinguish this from rollover risk, which arises when a lender refuses to renew a short-term loan.

Today: The Rise of the EIC


Bernstein
China, India, opium, tea, finance, coercion, and changing rules of trade.

Keay
How English merchants entered Asian trade and later accumulated political power.


Today asks how English merchants built a company with capacities usually associated with states.


Timing: 0–3 minutes. Reconnect to Monday. Bernstein showed the mature nineteenth-century system: the East India Company was central to production, finance, and imperial commerce. Keay takes us back to 1600 to show how merchants seeking access to distant markets built an organization that combined capital, monopoly, diplomacy, violence, information, and territorial authority.

text:
Your IB Voice

10 minutes · Individual · Notes permitted · No internet or LLMs


Commit to an explanation before we reconstruct the chapter.


Timing: 3–13 minutes. This prompt foregrounds the central contradiction in Keay. Students may explain the charter as a response to risk, Portuguese monopoly, Dutch competition, national interest, or the need for state-backed authority. Do not resolve it. Take answers on the next slide and treat them as hypotheses.
[Source] - Keay, Chapter 1, §ii–§iii.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: How did a nutmeg island become an imperial target?
text:
How did a nutmeg island become an imperial target?





Run was two miles long, had no fresh water, and produced nutmeg.

Its villages answered to no sultan. Councils of orang kaya governed each island as a self-governing republic.


Pulo Run had sovereignty of its own to give away.


Nutmeg tree (Myristica fragrans) © uforest.org


Timing: 17–20 minutes. Keay opens with Run because it makes the transition from trade to empire visible. The tree is Myristica fragrans. Keay describes it as “dark of foliage, willow-size, and carefully tended,” and notes it grew nowhere else on earth, which is the whole source of the rent. Establish the governance point now rather than later: thanks to their isolation the Banda islands “owed allegiance to no one,” authority rested with village councils under orang kaya, and in the tradition of adat each island was “a self-governing and fairly democratic republic.” They could “withhold or dispose of their sovereignty as they saw fit.” That is precisely why what happens in 1616 creates a legal problem the Company cannot absorb. Hold the 1616 pledge until the end of class.
[Sources] - Keay, Chapter 1, §i. - Map of the Banda Islands, Nationaal Archief / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: The prize was extraordinary
text:
The prize was extraordinary





<½ penny → £1.60


Ten pounds of nutmeg
Banda purchase price → European sale price



One-sixth of a ship’s cargo could pay for the entire voyage.


Nutmeg fruit with mace


Timing: 24–26 minutes. Use the photograph. Both commodities are visible in one fruit: the dark seed is the nutmeg, and the lacy scarlet membrane around it is the mace. Mace cost roughly ten times more per pound at both ends because one tree yields far less of it.
Lead with the prices rather than a percentage. Keay states a figure of roughly 32,000 per cent, but his own prices imply a larger multiple still. Nutmeg and mace produce the same ratio, so the percentage is best left off the slide.
The sixth-of-a-cargo line is the one students should retain. It explains the business logic behind the mortality figures introduced later: extreme risk was tolerable because expected returns were enormous.
[Source] - Keay, Chapter 1, §i–§ii.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Three forms of trade and sovereign power
text:
Three forms of trade and sovereign power


Portugal
A Crown enterprise
Capital: Crown and merchant contractors
Returns: Spice markups, customs, and licence fees to the Crown
Authority: Royal fleets, forts, and governors

The Dutch (VOC)
A sovereign company
Capital: Private shareholders
Returns: Dividends to investors; taxes and charter fees to the Dutch Republic
Authority: The VOC could make treaties, build forts, wage war, and govern territory

The English (EIC)
A more limited company
Capital: Private voyage subscribers
Returns: Profits to investors
Authority: Monopoly, factories, diplomacy, and armed ships, but no initial right to rule territory


All three fused commerce and state power. They differed in who paid, who profited, and who ruled.


Timing: 22–28 minutes. This slide does two jobs. Read the top half across as a comparison of institutional forms, then the bottom half across as the sequence that produced the English charter.
On the forms: do not imply all three were mature in 1600. Portugal’s system was long established, the English Company was chartered in December 1600, and the VOC in 1602.
Portugal ran a crown-administered maritime empire. Governors, fortified ports, and fleets controlled the strategic routes, and passing ships had to buy a licence from the Portuguese to trade — a system for taxing other people’s commerce without governing the territory it crossed. The claim rested on a papal grant that had divided the non-European world between Portugal and Spain, which is why the English regarded it as an “insolency” rather than a right. Papal authority linked Portugal’s commercial monopoly to conquest and the spread of Christianity. The papal bulls authorized conquest and colonization as well as trade and Christian evangelization.
The Dutch East India Company received extensive public powers from the Dutch Republic and combined commercial monopoly with treaties, armed conquest, and territorial rule, most brutally in the Banda Islands.
The English Company began with factories, diplomatic privileges, and armed shipping. Territorial and revenue-collecting government came much later, most consequentially in Bengal after 1765.
On the sequence: Keay is clear that Dutch success, not English ambition, was decisive. Lancaster’s 1591 reconnaissance had shown danger rather than profit. Dutch voyages in the late 1590s showed direct trade could pay, which doomed the Levant Company’s overland business. The final straw was news that the Dutch were buying English shipping, which let the petitioners argue that the national interest was at stake.
Note who the petitioners were: Muscovy and Levant Company men, “organized into powerful and exclusive syndicates with access to capital and influence, yet independent of both court and government.” That independence is about to come under pressure.
Asian rulers and merchants remained strategic actors throughout. The English entered an existing political economy rather than an open market.
[Sources] - Keay, Chapter 1, §i–iv. - Sanjay Subrahmanyam, The Portuguese Empire in Asia, 1500–1700, 2nd ed. (Wiley-Blackwell, 2012). - Femme S. Gaastra, The Dutch East India Company (Walburg Pers, 2003).

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Imperialism is broader than colonialism
text:
Imperialism is broader than colonialism


Imperialism
Extends effective control across territories and peoples.
It can operate through treaties, finance, monopoly, military force, or delegated company authority.
A local government may formally remain in place.

Colonialism
Places territory and people under sustained external rule.
Governing authority exercised by crown officials, settlers, or a chartered company.


An empire can dominate without establishing formal colonial rule. Colonialism entails assuming governance authority.


Timing: 20–22 minutes. Imperialism is the broader concept. It describes effective control exercised beyond a polity’s borders. That control can operate formally or informally through treaties, finance, commercial monopoly, military pressure, or authority delegated to a company. Local institutions may survive while their autonomy is sharply constrained.
Colonialism is a particular institutional form of imperialism. An external power assumes sustained authority over territory and people. Administration may be carried out by metropolitan officials, settlers, or a chartered company.
The distinction matters for Keay. Armed ships, exclusive trading rights, coercive seizures, and political treaties created imperial power before the East India Company governed a large colonial territory. Bantam remained a trading agency under a local ruler. Run raised a claim to territorial rule.
[Sources] - Michael W. Doyle, Empires (Cornell University Press, 1986), pp. 19, 30–47. - John Gallagher and Ronald Robinson, “The Imperialism of Free Trade,” Economic History Review 6, no. 1 (1953): 1–15. - Jürgen Osterhammel, Colonialism: A Theoretical Overview (Markus Wiener, 1997), pp. 15–20. - Keay, Chapter 1, §i–iv.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Around 1600, European trade was one layer of a larger Asian network
text:
Around 1600, European trade was one layer of a larger Asian network

European trade was one small part of a much larger Asian network.


Timing: 26–28 minutes. Let the map carry the argument. Trace the dense, overlapping routes linking East Africa, Aden and the Red Sea, Hormuz and the Persian Gulf, Indian textile ports, Malacca, the Indonesian spice islands, and China.
Keay’s narrative begins at the European edge of this system, but the system itself was predominantly Asian. Chinese, Malay, Indian, Arab, Persian, and other merchants had long connected regional production and consumption. Around 1600, the English were a small new entrant into these established circuits, not the network’s organizing center.
Avoid implying that European participation was inconsequential. Portuguese, Dutch, and English armed shipping increasingly changed access, prices, and political bargains. The chronological point is that this intervention entered and then reshaped a much older commercial world.
[Sources] - John Keay, The Honourable Company, Chapter 1, §ii. - Om Prakash, European Commercial Enterprise in Pre-Colonial India (Cambridge University Press, 1998), Chapters 1–5. - Simeon Netchev, “Map of the Trade in the Indian Ocean 15th–16th century,” World History Encyclopedia, 2025, CC BY-NC-ND: https://www.worldhistory.org/image/20178/map-of-the-trade-in-the-indian-ocean-15th-16th-cen/

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Frontier shipping became a question of national power
text:
Frontier shipping became a question of national power




Lancaster’s Red Dragon: 600 tons · 38 guns · built for privateering · about 200 men


Isaac Sailmaker, Two Views of an East Indiaman, c. 1685 · National Maritime Museum / Wikimedia Commons, public domain


A frontier capability
Ocean-going hulls combined cargo capacity, firepower, trained crews, and navigational knowledge.
The trigger
Dutch merchants then tried to buy English ships.
The political claim
The petitioners told Elizabeth that the “national interest” was at stake.


The Crown needed a way to harness privately assembled strategic capacity.


Timing: 31–34 minutes. The delay in granting the charter is not the teaching point. The important development is that English merchants and privateers had assembled a viable long-distance shipping capability that the Crown could neither ignore nor leave entirely to private or foreign control.
Treat frontier technology as a system, not simply a hull. Direct Asian trade depended on naval architecture, artillery, large pools of capital, trained mariners, navigational knowledge, provisioning, and command experience. Lancaster’s Red Dragon illustrates the platform: about 600 tons, 38 guns, built for privateering, and able to carry roughly 200 men. The painting is a later seventeenth-century East Indiaman rather than Lancaster’s actual ship, but it shows the armed merchant-ship form.
Keay identifies the trigger. Dutch voyages demonstrated that direct trade with Asia could be profitable. When Dutch merchants sought to add English shipping to their fleets, the English petitioners argued that the “national interest” was at stake and carried their petition to Queen Elizabeth. A privately created commercial capability had become strategically important to the state.
End with the transition: the next slide explains the royal charter as the instrument used to incorporate, privilege, constrain, and harness that capacity.
[Sources] - John Keay, The Honourable Company, Chapter 1, §ii–iv. - Isaac Sailmaker, Two Views of an East Indiaman of the Time of King William III, c. 1685, National Maritime Museum / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: The charter bestowed power
text:
The charter bestowed power
A royal charter was a sovereign grant creating a corporation and conferring legal privileges.


What it granted
Corporate status: continuity and internal governance
Monopoly: exclusive English trade beyond the Cape for 15 years
Enforcement: Company licenses; unlicensed trade risked forfeiture

Who gained
Subscribers: English rivals excluded; capital and voyage risk pooled
The Crown: privately financed maritime expansion; control over English participation


Merchants received monopoly returns while the Crown gained maritime authority.
