title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: The risk undertaken because the returns were large
text:
The risk undertaken because the returns were large





25 of 198


men who rounded the Cape on Lancaster’s 1591 voyage reached England again

On the first Company fleet, 105 of 480 men were dead before it reached the Cape.


Investors accepted these odds because one-sixth of a cargo still returned a profit.


Portrait of Sir James Lancaster · National Maritime Museum / Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 56–59 minutes. Two out of three ships were lost on Lancaster’s 1591 voyage. The only cargo to reach home was a boatload of scurvy victims. Keay writes that the experience should have discredited the project, but Dutch success revived investor interest.
On the first Company fleet, Lancaster prescribed three spoonfuls of lemon juice each morning aboard the Red Dragon. Its crew remained healthy through the scurvy latitudes while 105 men died before the Cape across the rest of the fleet. The remedy demonstrates a management problem: knowledge created value only when the organization adopted it beyond the individual commander.
Use the portrait to introduce Lancaster as a bundle of experience, reputation, and authority. His skills helped the Company operate, while dependence on one commander made the capability fragile.
[Sources] - Keay, Chapter 1, §iii–§iv. - Portrait of Sir James Lancaster, National Maritime Museum / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: At Aceh, Lancaster negotiated market access
text:
At Aceh, Lancaster negotiated market access




What Ala-uddin granted
A trading house, royal protection, full trading rights, and exemption from customs duties
What Elizabeth’s letter argued
No nation is self-sufficient, so distant countries should trade with one another.
Any prince who trades with only one European nation should expect political subordination to it.


England argued for open trade abroad while chartering a monopoly at home.


Theodor de Bry, Dutch envoys at Sultan Ala-uddin’s court, engraving published 1604 · Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 59–62 minutes. The engraving shows Dutch visitors at Ala-uddin’s court, not Lancaster’s audience. It was published in 1604 and depicts the same Sultan and court at the time of Lancaster’s 1602 visit. Make that distinction explicit.
Lancaster used court ritual, gifts, translation, and Elizabeth’s letter to secure a trading house, royal protection, trading privileges, and exemption from customs duties. He prostrated himself “after the manner of the country.”
Spend time on what the letter actually argued, because it is the sharpest irony in the chapter. In His “infinite and unsearchable wisdom” God had arranged that no nation be self-sufficient, so that “out of the abundance of ffruit which some region[s] enjoyeth, the necessitie or wante of others should be supplied.” Distant countries should therefore have “traffique” with one another and become friends through “their interchange of commodities.” The letter then turns pointed: Spain and Portugal insist on exclusive trading rights, and any prince who grants them “must expect a degree of political subordination to that nation.”
England was making the case for open trade as a challenger, two years after chartering a monopoly of its own, and was warning Asian rulers against precisely the exclusive arrangement the Company existed to build. Ask students to hold both facts at once rather than resolve them. The argument was also genuinely useful to Ala-uddin, whose rivalry with Portuguese Malacca made open trade his interest too, which is why Keay says the sentiments “could have been his own.” The letters were sent unaddressed, with the recipient’s name filled in by whoever delivered them, so the same doctrine was offered to every ruler the English met.
Connect forward: the free-trade argument reappears on Monday’s side of the course as the case against the Corn Laws, made by manufacturers who benefited from it. Arguments for open trade tend to be advanced by whoever is currently excluded.
Aceh had killed an objectionable Dutch commander two years earlier and had repeatedly challenged Portuguese Malacca. Ala-uddin was selecting among European partners rather than submitting to one.
The commercial result was limited because the expected pepper had not arrived. Keay describes Aceh’s importance as political and strategic rather than commercial.
[Sources] - Keay, Chapter 1, §ii and §iv, including the text of Elizabeth’s standard letter. - Theodor de Bry, Dutch visit to Sultan Ala-uddin’s court, engraving published 1604, Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Armed seizure solved England’s export problem
text:
Armed seizure solved England’s export problem




What Lancaster sailed with
£20,000 in Spanish silver
£6,000 in English goods
What he took by force
Indian textiles that more than doubled his trading stock


England had little to sell, so silver and seizure supplied what the market would take.


Portuguese India Armada of 1502, from the Livro de Lisuarte de Abreu, c. 1565 · Morgan Library / Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 64–67 minutes. The image depicts the Portuguese India Armada rather than Lancaster’s specific prize. Use it to establish the armed commercial system Lancaster entered.
Coercion was part of Lancaster’s strategy. On the 1591 reconnaissance voyage, Keay writes that no attempt was made to open honest trade. The targets included Asian and Portuguese shipping.
In 1602, Lancaster seized a Portuguese carrack carrying so many Indian calicoes that unloading took six days. Sultan Ala-uddin assisted by detaining a Portuguese emissary who might have raised the alarm. The captured textiles more than doubled Lancaster’s trading stock.
The cargo composition is the IB point. England made little that Southeast Asian merchants wanted. Lancaster carried bullion, then acquired Indian textiles that could purchase pepper and spices. Keay describes exploiting Asia’s existing carrying trade as an imperative.
[Sources] - Keay, Chapter 1, §iii–§iv. - Portuguese India Armada of 1502, Livro de Lisuarte de Abreu, c. 1565, Morgan Library / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Bantam was an early analogue of foreign direct investment
text:
Bantam was an early analogue of foreign direct investment




Without a factory
Each fleet arrival pushed spice prices up, pushed the price of its own cloth down, and left ships idle waiting for a return cargo.
With a factory
Resident factors bought and sold all year, so prices moved less and cargo was waiting when the fleet arrived.


Local presence changed the terms of every transaction the Company made.


View of Bantam, Java, early seventeenth century · Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 67–70 minutes. Separate the two mechanisms.
First, price effects. When a fleet arrived, it suddenly increased demand for spices and increased the local supply of imported cloth. Spice prices rose while prices for the Company’s cloth fell. Year-round factors could spread purchases and sales over time rather than transact at the fleet’s moment of maximum disadvantage.
Second, turnaround. Factors gathered information and assembled return cargo before the large ocean-going ships reached Bantam. The ships therefore spent less expensive time waiting in port.
Bantam is an early analogue of foreign direct investment because the Company replaced repeated export-market visits with a controlled, lasting commercial establishment abroad. Do not collapse the analogy into identity. The factory was a trading establishment rather than a modern incorporated affiliate or productive plant. It operated under a local ruler’s sovereignty and was not itself a colony.
[Sources] - John Keay, The Honourable Company, Chapter 1, §iv. - Peter J. Buckley and Mark Casson, The Future of the Multinational Enterprise (Macmillan, 1976). - View of Bantam, Java, Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: The Company depended on an existing Asian regional network
text:
The Company depended on an existing Asian regional network





Aceh: diplomacy and political access
Priaman: pepper
Bantam: factory and regional hub
Banda: nutmeg and mace
Moluccas: cloves and subsidiary voyages



The Bantam factory connected large Company ships to smaller Asian vessels carrying goods and market intelligence.


Locator map prepared for this course · Coastlines from the R maps package (CIA World Data Bank II) · Banda inset schematic, positions accurate


Timing: 70–73 minutes. Orient students on the map before making the argument. Aceh sits at the northern tip of Sumatra and Priaman farther down its west coast. Malacca lies across the straits on the Malay peninsula, which is why control of that channel mattered so much to the Portuguese. Bantam lies at the western end of Java on the Sunda Strait. The Banda Islands and the Moluccas lie far to the east.
The distances are the point students miss. Bantam to Banda is roughly 1,500 miles, covered in small vessels, and Run and Ai are so small that the inset has to enlarge them to make them visible at all. The whole nutmeg supply of the world came from a group about thirty miles across.
[The 1606 Hondius map of the East Indies remains in the repository as 2026-09-02-hondius-east-indies-1606.jpg if you would rather show the period cartography here or add it as a second slide.]
Keay calls the regional network the country trade: an “infinitely complex web of subsidiary voyages” in pinnaces, prahus, and junks, often commanded but rarely crewed by Europeans. These smaller vessels delivered produce and intelligence from remote ports and shallow waters to Company factories and ocean-going fleets.
Aceh supplied political access, while the Susan loaded pepper at Priaman. Bantam functioned as the hub: large ships connected it to England, while regional vessels connected it to the Banda Islands, Moluccas, and other Asian ports. The network created commercial capability and an auditing problem. Keay writes that it “invariably confounded the auditors but enriched the adventurers.”
The subsidiary voyage dispatched from Bantam toward the Moluccas in early 1603 brought the English to Pulo Run. The regional network therefore generated the later territorial claim.
[Sources] - Keay, Chapter 1, §iv. - Locator map generated by scripts/2026-09-02-eic-places-map.R; coastlines from the R maps package (CIA World Data Bank II).

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: The EIC did more than its charter mentioned
text:
The EIC did more than its charter mentioned


The charter created an English monopoly. EIC added diplomacy, armed seizure, and permanent foreign presence.


Timing: 73–75 minutes. Stop the timeline at 1603, the end of the first Company voyage.
Separate the authority granted in London from the capacities exercised abroad. The 1600 charter created an exclusive English trading organization with authority over its members and maritime conduct. Lancaster then negotiated with an Asian ruler, used armed force against Portuguese shipping, and left factors at a permanent trading agency.
None of these steps yet gave the Company authority to govern territory or populations. Ask which actions students nevertheless classified as imperial power. This preserves the distinction between imperial capacity and colonial rule and leaves the later transformation for the epilogue.
[Source] - John Keay, The Honourable Company, Chapter 1, §iii–iv.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Run turned trade into a territorial commitment
text:
Run turned trade into a territorial commitment





Threatened by the Dutch, Run’s leaders offered allegiance to the English in 1616 (English protection in echagne for nutmeg access).
The Company’s charter gave it no power to hold territory. The EIC accepted on the king’s behalf.
Four years of Dutch blockade later, the Company wanted rid of the island (too costly to defend), but King refused



Trade created demands for protection, turning a commercial relationship into a claim to colonial rule.


Map of the Banda Islands, copied from a chart found in 1602 · Nationaal Archief / Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 75–78 minutes. The pledge was sealed with a nutmeg seedling rooted in Run’s soil, which is worth telling aloud: seedlings were closely guarded and destroyed rather than surrendered, so handing one over was an act of real trust. Treat the pledge as a sovereign act by a self-governing polity choosing a protector under duress, after its neighbours had been coerced into Dutch control. Run places colonial rule on the table because the claim concerns territory, people, and governing authority.
Then the anticlimax, which is the honest ending. Keay: the island “never quite lived up to expectations” and “would become a fraught and expensive liability.” After a blockade lasting four years, the Company wanted to surrender Run. The Crown insisted on keeping “his exotic windfall and his Bandanese subjects.” The territorial prize was the authority the Company least wanted once it had it.
Close the loop on the activity: territorial authority belongs clearly in the imperial-power category and introduces colonial rule. The Company nevertheless tried to abandon Run when the territorial claim became a costly liability.
[Sources] - Keay, Chapter 1, §i. - Map of the Banda Islands, Nationaal Archief / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: The Company met each problem with organization or with force
text:
The Company met each problem with organization or with force







Cross-border problem
Company response




Portuguese and Dutch power restricted access
Charter, royal diplomacy, and armed ships


Voyages required capital and risk pooling
Capital subscribed one voyage at a time, then repaid when the ships returned


English exports found few Asian buyers
Bullion and country trade supplied tradable goods


Fleet arrivals distorted prices and delayed ships
Bantam factors traded year-round and prepared cargo




Timing: 81–84 minutes. Read each row from left to right and connect it to evidence already presented.
Portuguese and Dutch power restricted access to the spice trade. The English response combined an exclusive Crown charter, royal letters to Asian rulers, diplomacy at Aceh, and heavily armed ships. The 1600 charter created an English trading monopoly and internal Company government; it did not yet authorize territorial rule.
Long voyages required large amounts of capital and exposed investors to catastrophic loss. Subscriptions pooled capital for individual voyages, while centralized Company command organized the fleet. Permanent joint stock came later.
England made little that Southeast Asian markets wanted. Lancaster carried Spanish silver, seized Indian textiles, and exchanged those textiles for pepper. Country trade subsequently connected regional Asian markets and supplies.
Fleet arrivals simultaneously raised the price of spices the Company wanted to buy, lowered the price of the cloth it wanted to sell, and left ships waiting for cargo. Year-round factors spread transactions across time and prepared return cargo before the fleet arrived.
Distance made local knowledge indispensable but weakened oversight from London. Country trade extended the Company’s reach through Asian markets and carriers while increasing agent discretion and creating monitoring and auditing problems.
This is more precise than saying the Company simply internalized transactions. The EIC internalized selected coordinating functions while relying extensively on Asian merchants, carriers, rulers, and markets. Political authority was part of the organizational solution, not a separate contextual variable.
[Sources] - John Keay, The Honourable Company, Chapter 1, §ii–§iv. - Ronald H. Coase, “The Nature of the Firm,” Economica 4, no. 16 (1937): 386–405. - Peter J. Buckley and Mark Casson, The Future of the Multinational Enterprise (Macmillan, 1976).

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Epilogue: from Spice Race to Colonialism
text:
Epilogue: from Spice Race to Colonialism


Territorial revenue extraction made permanent military power self-financing.


Timing: 78–81 minutes. This is a contingent sequence, not an automatic evolution from factory to colony.
Permanent establishments created sunk assets and security commitments. Fortified settlements and European rivalry pulled Company agents into military competition and political alliances. In eighteenth-century India, the Company intervened in regional conflicts using Indian allies, financiers, intermediaries, and predominantly Indian sepoy armies.
The decisive transition was fiscal. Victories at Plassey in 1757 and Buxar in 1764 preceded the 1765 grant of the diwani, the right to collect the revenues of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. The Company could now use territorial taxation to finance permanent military power. Revenue funded armies; armies secured additional territory and revenue. The trading company became a military-fiscal company state governing populations.
Financial crisis, corruption, and administrative failure brought the British state further inside Company government. The Regulating Act of 1773 and Pitt’s India Act of 1784 imposed increasing parliamentary supervision. After the rebellion of 1857, the Government of India Act 1858 transferred the Company’s territories, revenues, armies, and administrative powers to the Crown. That was the transition from Company colonialism to Crown colonialism, not the beginning of colonialism.
The VOC demonstrates that the path could unfold earlier and differently. Its destruction of Jayakarta and creation of Batavia in 1619, followed by the conquest of Banda in 1621, converted chartered commercial powers into colonial coercion in the spice-producing islands. The English Company’s path in India took longer and turned on control of territorial revenue.
[Sources] - John Keay, The Honourable Company, Chapter 1, §i–iv. - Philip J. Stern, The Company-State: Corporate Sovereignty and the Early Modern Foundations of the British Empire in India (Oxford University Press, 2011). - UK Parliament, “Parliament and the East India Company.” - UK Parliament, “East India Company and Raj, 1785–1858.” - Rijksmuseum, “The Dutch East India Company (VOC).”

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: The EIC is an ancestor of the modern MNE
text:
The EIC is an ancestor of the modern MNE


Chartered company

Permanent factories placed Company agents and assets abroad
Charter, diplomacy, and armed force supported trade
Commercial activity generated claims over territory and people


Modern multinational

FDI creates a lasting interest and managerial influence abroad
Market access is governed by host-state law and trade and investment rules
Firms face political risk but normally lack sovereign authority



The continuity is organization across distance. Modern law more sharply separates corporate authority from sovereign power.


Timing: 84–86 minutes. Make a bounded comparison. The EIC belongs in the history of multinational organization because it pooled capital, coordinated distant agents, maintained overseas establishments, and operated across several markets. It is not a modern multinational in institutional form.
The Crown granted exclusive access to English merchants, sent letters to foreign rulers, and tolerated or authorized armed commercial action in wartime. Company activities generated claims to public authority, including Run’s pledge of allegiance. Later charters expanded the Company’s authority to hold and govern territory.
Modern multinational firms organize foreign affiliates through corporate law, ownership, contracts, and managerial hierarchy. Their access is structured by host-state law and international trade and investment rules. They bargain with governments and face political risk, but they do not normally possess legal authority to wage war, negotiate sovereign treaties, or govern populations.
The current IB lesson is therefore specific. Cross-border firms still solve problems of capital, information, local adaptation, and control. The EIC solved them through an institutional bundle that joined corporate and sovereign power much more closely than modern law ordinarily permits.
[Sources] - Keay, Chapter 1, §i–§iv. - Peter J. Buckley and Mark Casson, The Future of the Multinational Enterprise (Macmillan, 1976). - Jean J. Boddewyn and Thomas L. Brewer, “International-Business Political Behavior: New Theoretical Directions,” Academy of Management Review 19, no. 1 (1994): 119–143.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Reflection: Return to your IB Voice
text:
Reflection: Return to your IB Voice

Why did England organize Asian trade through a monopoly company rather than through competing merchants or direct Crown control?


Revisit your opening answer: explain what the charter solved and what new political problem it created.


Timing: 86–89 minutes. Return students to the claim they made at the beginning of class. Ask for one revision grounded in evidence from the lecture.
Strong answers should distinguish the merchants’ need for pooled capital, exclusivity, and sovereign backing from the Crown’s interest in English shipping capacity, strategic competition, and control over English participation. The cost of the bargain might include excluded merchants, the pressure of Court patronage, English rivals who traded in defiance of the monopoly, private coercion, or the later expansion of delegated authority.
Do not require consensus about which side needed the other more. The purpose is to make students revise an initial causal judgment using evidence.
[Source] - Keay, Chapter 1, §ii–iv.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Lessons learned this week
text:
Lessons learned this week


1. States carve out markets
The charter and the Canton system decided who could trade. Commerce then acquired armies and territory.
2. Open trade has losers, and they fight
Corn Laws Repeal enriched manufacturers and cost landowners. Dutch displacement led to embargo.
3. Institutions determine who wins
The same argument loses in a landowners’ Parliament and wins in 1846. A monopoly charter bestows market exclusivity.

4. Ideas need political translators
Smith/Ricardo defined the logic of trade. Cobden’s League and a famine shaped politics. Lancaster partied and shared the Queen’s letter.
5. Incentives for the illicit
Seized carracks, opium. Norms, law, and weapons imperfectly constrain.
6. State and commercial power reinforce each other
Commercial power extends state reach; state power protects commercial advantage.


Timing: 89–90 minutes. These are claims about how markets and political authority produce each other, not a summary of the narrative. Each one should be arguable.
On the first, the point is that the market did not exist prior to the authority that defined it. A charter, a Portuguese trading licence, and the Canton system are three different instruments for the same act: deciding who may trade, where, and with whom. The second sentence is the harder half. Once commerce holds a privilege it starts acquiring the means to defend it, so the Company accumulated armed shipping, treaty-making, and eventually territory and revenue. Commercial interest and coercive authority did not stay separate spheres that occasionally touched; they fused into a single organisation. Ask students where the line between firm and state actually falls in 1616, or in 1765.
On the second, resist the framing of free trade as efficiency against ignorance. Repeal moved income from landowners to manufacturers and to consumers of bread, and the losers understood that perfectly well, which is why they held it off for three decades. Every trade regime creates a distribution, and the fight is over who gets to set it. This is also the honest reading of Elizabeth’s letter: England argued for open trade where it was excluded and for monopoly where it was not.
On the third, the venue is not neutral. The same economic argument that persuades an economist fails in a Parliament elected on a franchise that over-represents landowners, and succeeds once the coalition and the crisis change. Institutions determine whose preferences get counted. The charter, Parliament, and the later Regulating and India Acts are all venues in which particular interests were advantaged by design.
On the fourth, ideas do not travel on their own merit. Smith and Ricardo supplied the analytical case decades before repeal, and nothing happened. What moved policy was Cobden’s organised campaign, the money and membership behind it, and then a famine that made the political cost of protection unbearable. Rhetoric, resources, and shock did the work that argument alone could not. Say plainly that this is not an argument that ideas are irrelevant, only that they are insufficient.
On the fifth, high returns pull activity toward whatever the law does not reach. Lancaster took a Portuguese carrack by force, Company servants ran the country trade partly on their own account, and private traders carried opium into a market that had banned it. In each case the profit was legal or illegal depending on which authority you asked. This is where norms and ethics enter the course rather than as a coda: the constraint on commercial behaviour is whatever combination of law, enforcement, and professional norm actually binds, and all three were weak at a distance of six months’ sail.
[Sources] - William J. Bernstein, A Splendid Exchange, Chapter 11. - John Keay, The Honourable Company, Chapter 1, “Islands of Spicerie.”

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Bernstein and Keay address different questions
text:
Bernstein and Keay address different questions


August 31 · Bernstein
How are trade rules created, contested, evaded, and changed?
Restricted access · illicit commerce · domestic conflict · coercion

September 2 · Keay
What kind of organization made this trade possible?
Risk · chartered monopoly · armed commerce · delegated authority


Today we study political conflict over trade. Wednesday we dive into corporate power.


Timing: 0–3 minutes. Explain the fixed reading sequence. Bernstein begins with the mature political economy of long-distance trade: restricted access, monopoly, illicit commerce, distributional conflict, coercion, and changing rules. Keay then steps back to explain the organizational form that made such trade possible and accumulated quasi-state powers. Do not resolve the EIC organizational puzzle today.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Your IB Voice
text:
Your IB Voice


Question


Britain and China had traded at Canton for over a century without war. In 1839 they went to war. What changed? Defend your answer with evidence from the reading.



10 minutes · Individual · Notes allowed · No internet or LLMs


Timing: 3–13 minutes. Ask students to choose a primary explanation and defend it with chapter evidence. The purpose is to generate competing hypotheses before the lecture reconstructs the sequence. Do not resolve the question. Strongest answer is roughly: enforcement became urgent for Beijing at the same moment restraint disappeared on the British side, and the confiscation turned a smuggling dispute into a Crown liability.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Hypotheses
text:
Hypotheses

What explains the war?


Take each one: was it also true in 1780?


Timing: MM–MM minutes.
Take four or five answers and write each on the board as a short phrase. Do not sort or group them. Then advance to reveal the second question and work down the board one hypothesis at a time. Anything true in 1780 has a timing problem the student needs to solve; anything that is not is a candidate cause, so ask that student what set it off when it did. Leave the board list standing for the rest of class.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Canton permitted trade on Qing terms
text:
Canton permitted trade on Qing terms





The Qing state confined Western foreign trade to Canton and licensed Chinese hongs (merchant houses).

The aim was to keep silver at home and foreign influence out.

Qing authorities used the Canton system to control the terms of foreign trade.



William Daniell, View of the Canton Factories, 1805–06 · Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 18–22 minutes. Define the Canton System through three controls: where foreigners could trade, through whom, and under what conditions. Explain that concern about silver outflows is recognizably mercantilist, while the broader objective is sovereignty: obtain gains from trade while limiting foreign penetration, dependence, and political influence.
[Sources] - William J. Bernstein, A Splendid Exchange, Chapter 11, pp. 284–287. - William Daniell, View of the Canton Factories, 1805–06, Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Britain paid for tea with silver
text:
Britain paid for tea with silver



≈90%


of the value Britain sent to China was bullion


In 1751, Britain sent £119,000 in silver and £10,842 in merchandise.
Britain bought tea and silk. China bought little that Britain made.


The imbalance created pressure to find something China would buy.


Timing: 22–25 minutes. Bernstein reports that roughly 90 percent of the value of eighteenth-century British exports to China was bullion and provides the 1751 example. Ask whether the imbalance itself necessarily causes conflict or becomes dangerous through the responses it induces.
[Source] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 286–287.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Mercantilism linked commerce to national power
text:
Mercantilism linked commerce to national power
State power: Commerce should strengthen the state
Bullion: Gold and silver supported public credit, military spending, and political power
Trade balance: Export surpluses brought bullion into the country
Empire: Colonies and chartered companies like EIC secured supplies, markets, shipping

Britain bought Chinese goods with silver while China bought little British merchandise. Mercantilists saw the outflow as a loss of national wealth and power.


Timing: 18–21 minutes. Define mercantilism as a view of commerce shaped by national power and rivalry. Bullion mattered because it supported public credit, military spending, and the fiscal capacity of the state. Mercantilists did not oppose all imports. Imports that strengthened national production or power could be valuable. Their concerns were dependency, bullion loss, and whether trade strengthened another state more than their own. Use this framework to explain why Britain’s persistent silver outflow to China appeared to require a solution.
[Sources] - William J. Bernstein, A Splendid Exchange, Chapter 11, pp. 284–287. - Lars Magnusson, The Political Economy of Mercantilism (Routledge, 2015). - Francis Swaine, An East Indiaman in Stays, c. 1780, Royal Museums Greenwich / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: From cotton to opium
text:
From cotton to opium





The EIC grew and auctioned opium in India. Private traders carried it into China.


The increased imports led to silver outflows from China, which they tried to halt



Opium factory at Patna, c. 1851 · Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 25–30 minutes. Explain the triangle briefly before the opium step: the EIC’s position in Bengal gave it Indian cotton, which China bought, so Britain routed trade through India to cover its bilateral imbalance with China; when Chinese demand for Indian cotton weakened, the commercial search continued and opium took cotton’s place. Then distinguish the Company’s legal position in India from the private traders’ illicit entry into China. The analytical point is strategic response: commercial and political actors chose an organizational solution to the imbalance.
[Sources] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 287–290. - Opium factory at Patna, c. 1851, Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Barriers created rents and rewarded evasion
text:
Barriers created rents and rewarded evasion


Regulation redirected commerce through smugglers and intermediaries.


Timing: 30–33 minutes. Define rents as returns created by restricted access or an artificial price wedge. Chinese controls did not remove demand for market access; they encouraged organizational separation, intermediaries, smuggling, and illicit commerce. Save contemporary analogies for the end.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Production and finance kept the EIC at the center
text:
Production and finance kept the EIC at the center




The Company auctioned opium in India.
Private traders sold it in China for silver.
The silver bought Company bills.
EIC silver bought tea.

Infrastructural power: the EIC never carried opium into China, yet every stage of the trade ran through it.



The Opium Trade in China, 1833–1839 · MIT Visualizing Cultures


Timing: 33–37 minutes. Walk through the four steps of the circuit on the slide. Then ask the question the slide implies: how did the EIC shape an illegal trade that private merchants conducted? Introduce “infrastructural power”: the capacity to shape production, finance, and exchange without directing every transaction. Pose the organizational puzzle but do not solve it. Keay explains the origins of this capacity on September 2.
[Sources] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 287–291. - MIT Visualizing Cultures, The Opium Trade in China, 1833–1839.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Lin Zexu turned tension into crisis
text:
Lin Zexu turned tension into crisis



40,000


chests of opium a year by the late 1830s, four times the 1825 level



In 1839, Commissioner Lin detained foreign merchants and destroyed more than 20,000 chests of opium.

To the Qing court, this was enforcement of Chinese law and sovereignty.
To British merchants, it was an attack on property and commerce.


Timing: 37–42 minutes. Start with the numbers: the EIC lost its China monopoly in 1834, private firms such as Jardine Matheson combined the country trade with the tea trade, and Bernstein reports growth from roughly 10,000 to 40,000 chests. Removing one monopoly did not make the trading system lawful or apolitical. Lin’s intervention followed arrests of local smugglers and mounting social and fiscal consequences. Ask students to give the strongest account of each interpretation. The enforcement shock is endogenous: it arose from consequences produced by the trading regime itself.
[Source] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 290–297.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Commercial interests mobilized military power
text:
Commercial interests mobilized military power





Merchants lobbied London for compensation and wider access. The government sent warships.


Britain’s use of military force to expand market access led to interstate conflict: the Opium War.



E. Duncan, The Nemesis Destroying Chinese War Junks, 1843 · National Maritime Museum / MIT Visualizing Cultures


Timing: 42–45 minutes. Jardine and other merchants pressed the British cabinet for a favorable treaty backed by naval force. The Nemesis was built for the EIC and designed for shallow Chinese waters. Emphasize the political translation from commercial grievance to state coercion.
[Sources] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 297–302. - E. Duncan, The Nemesis Destroying Chinese War Junks, 1843, National Maritime Museum / MIT Visualizing Cultures.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: The Treaty of Nanking rewrote the rules of trade
text:
The Treaty of Nanking rewrote the rules of trade


Indemnity · Hong Kong · five treaty ports · end of the hong monopoly · (eventually) low tariffs


John Platt and John Burnet, The Signing of the Treaty of Nanking, 1846 · Anne S. K. Brown Military Collection / Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 45–48 minutes. No provision legalized opium. The treaty nevertheless changed market access, tariff authority, and territorial control; subsequent agreements expanded British privileges. Return briefly to the opening hypotheses: the imbalance was a pressure, restrictions shaped the response, commercial interests mobilized, and coercive state power changed the rules.
[Sources] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 302–304. - John Platt and John Burnet, The Signing of the Treaty of Nanking, 1846, Anne S. K. Brown Military Collection / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: The Long Path to More Open Trade
text:
The Long Path to More Open Trade


Sovereignty → trade restrictions → rents → circumvention


Crackdown → interstate conflict → forced rule change


Responses to the trade imbalance transformed commercial tensions into interstate conflict.


Timing: 48–51 minutes. Abstract the mechanism only after reconstructing the case. This is one pathway: controlled access generates circumvention; growing consequences provoke enforcement; enforcement triggers interstate conflict; power then produces forced rule change.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: What did the Corn Laws actually do?
text:
What did the Corn Laws actually do?





Who is protected when wheat prices fall below 63 shillings? Who pays?



Bernstein, A Splendid Exchange, Chapter 11, Table 11-1


Timing: 51–54 minutes. Ask students to read the schedule before explaining it. When the domestic wheat price fell below 63 shillings, the 24.25-shilling import levy made foreign grain much more expensive. The rule protected domestic landowners and grain prices while raising food costs for consumers. Use their answers to introduce the distributional positions on the next slide.
[Source] - William J. Bernstein, A Splendid Exchange, Chapter 11, Table 11-1.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Free-trade ideas became a political program
text:
Free-trade ideas became a political program

Smith and Ricardo showed that protection raised costs and blocked gains from trade. Cobden’s League organized that argument into a campaign for repeal.

The League turned an abstract economic argument into policy.


Timing: 54–58 minutes. Comparative advantage appears here as part of the ideas component. Smith and Ricardo supplied a framework. Cobden and the Anti-Corn Law League converted it into a campaign. Landowner interests and parliamentary influence kept repeal blocked until 1845.
[Source] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 305–312.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Prepare a 30-second statement for the public hearing
text:
Prepare a 30-second statement for the public hearing


5 minutes · Individual · Notes permitted


Maintain, modify, or repeal? Consider your two strongest arguments, who gains and who loses, and the strongest argument against your position.


Timing: 58–65 minutes. Physically divide the room into three sides. Assign students rather than allowing self-selection if one side is sparse. They are not formal groups: every student prepares an individual argument and may be called on. Establish the material stakes as you assign sides: landowners held concentrated interests and disproportionate institutional influence, industrialists were a rising economic constituency, and urban workers and consumers bore higher food costs without equivalent political power. Then circulate and press students to distinguish material interests, public arguments, and political leverage. Do not mention the famine.
[Source] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 305–312.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Public hearing
text:
Public hearing

Should Britain maintain, modify, or repeal the Corn Laws?


We will hear from each side. Listen for interests, expected winners and losers, political influence, and ideas.


Timing: 65–74 minutes. Cold-call multiple students from each side for short testimony and rebuttal. On the board, sort claims under material interests, winners and losers, political influence, and arguments or ideas. Surface the stable protectionist equilibrium without yet naming shocks as the lesson.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Round 2
text:
Round 2

Does the shock change your position?

If yes, what changed in your reasoning? If no, how do you defend the existing policy now?

2 minutes · Individual reconsideration


Timing: 75–80 minutes. Give students two minutes, then take brief testimony from each side. Ask whether the shock changed material interests, moral and political costs, expectations about governing survival, or the viability of the existing coalition.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: The famine raised the political cost of protection
text:
The famine raised the political cost of protection

Landowners gained from protection and dominated Parliament. But repeal was a known possibility already circulating in political debate.

The crisis fractured the governing coalition and made repeal possible.


Timing: 80–83 minutes. Interests and institutions remained in place. The shock raised the political cost of protection, strengthened an available policy alternative, and enabled political realignment under Peel.
[Source] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 310–312.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Two pathways made trade rules unstable
text:
Two pathways made trade rules unstable


China
Restrictions
→ circumvention
→ crackdown
→ interstate conflict
→ forced rule change

Corn Laws
Distributional conflict
→ durable coalition
→ external shock
→ political realignment
→ liberalization


Rules create rents, coalitions defend them, institutions sustain them, and ideas plus shocks change them.


Timing: 83–87 minutes. Do not force the cases into one identical model. China’s enforcement shock emerged from the consequences of the trade regime and led to coercive interstate change. The famine was an external shock that changed domestic coalition politics. Then read the key line as the conceptual payoff: interests supply preferences; institutions weight those preferences; ideas supply interpretations and alternatives; shocks change the political costs and coalition possibilities. Ask students to name the actor, institution, idea, and destabilizing event in each case. Neither markets nor policy changes are self-executing, and repeal was political change, not the automatic implementation of economic truth.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: The same mechanisms shape international business today
text:
The same mechanisms shape international business today







18th and 19th Centuries
International business today




Mercantilism and controlled access
Economic security and strategic sovereignty


Smuggling and intermediaries
Transshipment and sanctions evasion


EIC production and financial infrastructure
Big Tech dominance


Corn Law coalition and famine
Sectoral lobbying and crisis-driven realignment




When states constrain globalization, firms reorganize trade around the new limits.


Timing: 87–89 minutes. Keep the analogies brief. The claim is not that history repeats or that the cases are equivalent. The recurring mechanisms are controlled access, rents, circumvention, infrastructural power, distributional coalitions, and shock-driven realignment.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: The EIC puzzle remains
text:
The EIC puzzle remains

What kind of company could organize trade, finance, coercion, and political authority across continents?


On Wednesday we ask why long-distance trade required a chartered company and how that company acquired such immense power.


Timing: 89–90 minutes. Return to the unresolved EIC puzzle. Monday established the Company’s infrastructural capacity. Keay explains how long-distance risk and organizational problems produced the chartered-company form, and how capabilities created for commerce became foundations of political power and empire.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Module 3: what makes international (“cross-border”) business costly?
text:
Module 3: what makes international (“cross-border”) business costly?



Geographic friction
Today: containerization
Freight · time · handling · coordination


Border friction
Next: currencies · jurisdictions · trade rules
Exchange rates · legal systems · trade policy · political risk


Kees Torn / Wikimedia Commons · U.S. Customs and Border Protection


Timing: 0-3. Module map: distance today, currencies tomorrow, jurisdictions 14th, trade rules 16th.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Your IB Voice
text:
Your IB Voice


Question


Levinson says the container’s value lies in how it is used. What exactly did the box change, and why did its largest effects take a decade to appear?



10 minutes · Individual · Notes permitted


Commit to one causal explanation before we investigate the system.


Timing: 3-13. Want a named cost or capability, not “shipping got cheaper.” Do not resolve.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Interrogate the explanations
text:
Interrogate the explanations

What changed immediately when cargo entered a box?


What changed only after the surrounding system was rebuilt?


Timing: 13-17. Take four or five answers onto the board unsorted. Then reveal the second question and work down the list. Leave the board standing for the return at the end.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Cargo crossed the port one piece at a time
text:
Cargo crossed the port one piece at a time




Each handoff consumed labor and time, exposed cargo to loss, and required another organization to coordinate.

The port was the expensive break in the journey.



Breakbulk loading, Brooklyn, 1967 · Library of Congress


Timing: 17-20. Ask what costs are visible in the photograph.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: In the chapter example, ports were nearly half the cost
text:
In the chapter example, ports were nearly half the cost


A dozen vendors moved one truckload of medicine from Chicago to France circa 1960. The two ports alone cost $1,163 of the $2,386 total.


Levinson, The Box, Chapter 1, Table 1


Timing: 20-24. Table 1: total $2,386. Ports $1,163 (48.7%). Ocean $581 (24.4%). Inland 22.9% combined. One estimated shipment, not an average.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Before containerization, freight could rival trade barriers
text:
Before containerization, freight could rival trade barriers

In 1961, U.S. exporters spent about 12 cents of every export dollar on ocean freight.




12%


ocean freight as a share of U.S. export value



7%


average U.S. import tariff



Moving goods across oceans could cost more than the formal tariff barrier.


Timing: 24-27. These are scale comparisons rather than identical measures: freight is reported against export value, while the tariff is the average duty on imports. Levinson also notes that freight added 13% to steel pipe shipped from New York to Brazil and $20 to a refrigerator shipped from London to Cape Town.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Fifty-eight boxes sailed from Newark in 1956
text:
Fifty-eight boxes sailed from Newark in 1956




Separated the container from the truck chassis and designed a continuous handoff among truck, ship, and rail.


Ideal-X, 1956 · Maersk/SeaLand


Timing: 27-31. April 26, 1956. Newark to Houston. McLean was a trucker.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: One fitting made different networks compatible
text:
One fitting made different networks compatible





A standard corner casting lets cranes, chassis, rail cars, and ships handle the same box.

Compatibility required common standards for dimensions, fittings, strength, identification, and operating rules.
The corner fitting itself is standardized under ISO 1161.


ArnoldReinhold / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0


Timing: 31-34. ISO/TC 104 formed 1961. ISO R668 on dimensions accepted 1968. Neither date is in Levinson.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: ISO: who sets international standards?
text:
ISO: who sets international standards?


What?
An independent, nongovernmental organization whose members are national standards bodies.
Where?
Its Central Secretariat is in Geneva, Switzerland.
When?
ISO was founded in 1947. Its freight-container committee, TC 104, was created in 1961.
Why?
Common voluntary standards let firms and countries build compatible products and infrastructure without a single company controlling the system.




Relevant here: ISO/R 668:1968 established the core classification, dimensions, and ratings for Series 1 freight containers.


ISO · Geneva headquarters · ISO/R 668:1968


Timing: 34-38. ISO officially came into existence in 1947 to coordinate and unify standards developed by national standards bodies. It remains an independent, nongovernmental organization, with a Central Secretariat in Geneva. TC 104 was created in 1961 for freight containers. ISO/R 668:1968 was the first published version of the standard that evolved into today’s ISO 668, covering Series 1 freight-container classification, dimensions, and ratings. The IB point is interoperability: once firms could rely on common dimensions and ratings, they could invest in compatible ships, cranes, rail cars, chassis, and terminals.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: A container port operates like a factory
text:
A container port operates like a factory



Panama · Course photograph


Timing: 34-38. 1,400-foot ship, 9,000 forty-foot boxes, crew of 20. Cranes move 30 to 40 boxes an hour. Ship gone in 24 hours.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: The box reduced five costs at once
text:
The box reduced five costs at once


Containerization lowered total landed cost by reducing handling, delay, risk, and coordination costs as well as freight charges.


Timing: 38-42. The just-in-time claim is Levinson’s strongest and is asserted rather than shown. A group contests it in the exercise.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Malaysia to Cincinnati in 28 days, unopened
text:
Malaysia to Cincinnati in 28 days, unopened


Economists: it is now better to assume that moving goods is essentially costless than to assume it is an important component of production.


Timing: 42-45. 9,000 miles to Los Angeles in 23 days, 11,000 miles and 28 days door to door, under the price of one business-class ticket.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Why the payoff took a decade
text:
Why the payoff took a decade


The payoff waited for standards, infrastructure, organizational redesign, and agreements over dock labor, port investment, and regulation.


Edison had the incandescent bulb by 1879. Twenty years later, 3 percent of American homes had electric light.



Edison lamp · Smithsonian Institution


Timing: 45-51. “Political bargains” means concrete agreements over who bore the costs of transition: union work rules and compensation for dock labor, public and private investment in new terminals, and regulatory approval for new shipping practices. Ask who could organize against the change. Dockworkers, ship lines, and incumbent ports had concentrated losses.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Ricardo’s model assumed away shipping costs
text:
Ricardo’s model assumed away shipping costs





Ricardo’s 1817 wine-and-cloth example compared production costs in England and Portugal. Moving the goods between them cost nothing in the model.


Comparative advantage explains why specialization can create gains. Transport costs help determine whether specialization across distance is viable.



David Ricardo, c. 1821 · Thomas Phillips / National Portrait Gallery


Timing: 51-54. A qualification, not a refutation. Ricardo intentionally abstracted from transport costs. Modern economic geography puts distance, transport costs, and location closer to the center of the analysis.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Multinational plants became one production network
text:
Multinational plants became one production network


Firms could reorganize production across viable locations as wages, exchange rates, capabilities, and other conditions changed.


Timing: 57-61. Distinguish a multinational, which owns plants in several countries, from a network, in which each plant specializes and they exchange components.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Fragmented production created two core IB decisions
text:
Fragmented production created two core IB decisions


Where?
Where should each activity take place?
Wages · skills · infrastructure · market access · risk

Who?
Who should perform it?
The firm itself · an outside supplier


Lower trade costs expanded the set of viable locations and suppliers. We will study this later in the semester.


Timing: 61-63. This is the bridge to the standard IB questions of location, offshoring, outsourcing, and ownership. Keep it brief here; those choices return later in the course.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Trade surged, but causation remains difficult
text:
Trade surged, but causation remains difficult



2×


manufactured trade grew more than twice as fast as manufacturing output in the decade after 1966


What else changed?
Tariffs · exchange rates · oil shocks · computers

How could we isolate the container’s effect?



Propose a comparison that could separate the container from the other changes.


Timing: 63-68. Manufactured trade grew 2x manufacturing output and 2.5x global output in the decade after 1966. Push for research designs, not for more data: a constant shipment priced over time, similar routes containerized at different dates, trade around port conversion.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: The same people gained as consumers and faced new competition at work
text:
The same people gained as consumers and faced new competition at work


As consumers
4× more imported product varieties in the United States, 2002 vs. 1972
Estimated gain from added variety: nearly 3% of GDP

At work
Export hubs gained jobs and investment.
Import-competing workers faced more distant competitors.


France: some manufacturers shifted production abroad rather than absorb the cost of a shorter workweek with unchanged pay.



Consumer gains were broad. Employment losses were concentrated in particular occupations and places.


Timing: 66-70. Individuals occupy both roles: consumers and workers. Four times the imported varieties by 2002 against 1972; estimated benefit near 3 percent of GDP. Keep the France example as an illustration of firms gaining a credible relocation option.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Containerization relocated the port economy
text:
Containerization relocated the port economy




Port Newark, 1996 · SCI Archives



New York’s finger piers lacked the contiguous land and surface connections container terminals required.

Port activity shifted to large terminals at Newark and Elizabeth, New Jersey, just west of New York City. Waterfront employment and investment moved with it.


Timing: 70-74. Elizabeth is in northeastern New Jersey, immediately south of Newark, and forms part of the Port Newark-Elizabeth Marine Terminal complex. The regional port survived; activity moved from Manhattan and Brooklyn piers to larger New Jersey terminals. Liverpool declined. Busan, Seattle, Felixstowe, and Tanjung Pelepas rose.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: What still resists distance?
text:
What still resists distance?
Running shoes · fresh flowers · cars · cement · accounting software · haircuts

Rank them from easiest to hardest to serve from 5,000 miles away. For each, name the transport or coordination cost that drives your ranking.


Value-to-weight, perishability, transport mode, and the need for face-to-face delivery still shape what can be traded over distance.


Timing: 74-80. Volunteers only. Use the examples to separate different physical frictions. Running shoes travel well in containers. Fresh flowers rely on air freight and cold chains. Cars use roll-on, roll-off vessels. Cement is heavy and low-value relative to weight. Accounting software moves digitally. Haircuts require co-location.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Cheap freight did not erase location
text:
Cheap freight did not erase location


Containerization changed
Handling · inventory · reliability · coordination

Border frictions still divide markets
Currencies · jurisdictions · trade rules · political risk


Why do firms keep production in high-wage locations?


Timing: 80-83. Define border frictions here for the first time: costs created by crossing national boundaries rather than by physical distance itself. Two or three rapid answers on the closing question. Tomorrow begins with currencies.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: 1985 without containerization
text:
1985 without containerization

Cargo still crosses ports piece by piece. Jet travel, computers, oil shocks, and tariff reductions are unchanged.




Japanese cars in the United States
Walmart
Shenzhen manufacturing
Toyota just-in-time production



New York garment district decline
Nespresso capsule
Bangalore software services
Kenyan cut flowers



10 minutes · Groups of four
Without containerization, is your example mostly unchanged · later/smaller · unlikely in this form?
Name one mechanism that explains your choice.


Timing: 85-101. Assign one case per group. Likely mostly unchanged: Japanese cars, Toyota JIT, Bangalore software, Kenyan flowers. Likely later/smaller: Walmart, New York garments, Nespresso. Shenzhen may generate a useful argument between later/smaller and unlikely in this form. Traps: cars cross on roll-on, roll-off vessels; Toyota developed JIT before containerization; Bangalore depends on telecommunications; Kenyan flowers move by air. Push students to name the mechanism linking containerization to the outcome.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Reflection: return to your IB Voice
text:
Reflection: return to your IB Voice

What exactly did the box change, and why did its largest effects take a decade to appear?


Revise your opening answer. Which link in your causal argument changed?


Standards, complementary investment, organizational change, and policy lowered total landed cost. Global competition and fragmented production followed.


Tomorrow: one production network, many currencies.


Timing: 106-108. Mark one sentence in the opening response and write a revised version beneath it.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: A wealthy region cut community college classes
text:
A wealthy region cut community college classes




Coolcaesar, 2006 · Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.


Cupertino, 2012
De Anza had cut more than 1,000 courses and 8% of its faculty since 2008.
Nearby Apple reported rising profits.


Duhigg and Kocieniewski, NYT, April 28, 2012


Today: how firms reduce taxes, and what that means for the communities where they operate.


Timing: 0–3 minutes.
Locate the college near Apple’s headquarters. Explain that the NYT pairs corporate prosperity with a public funding crisis; it identifies several causes of California’s shortfall. Introduce the question of corporate responsibility before explaining tax mechanisms.
[Sources]
Duhigg and Kocieniewski, NYT, April 28, 2012, supplied PDF pp. 1–3, 11–13.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Your IB Voice
text:
Your IB Voice


Question


Should Apple use every legal means available to minimize its tax bill? Address the strongest objection to your argument, considering Apple’s responsibilities to shareholders and the communities where it operates.



10 minutes · Individual · Notes permitted · No internet or LLMs


Timing: 3–13 minutes.
Keep the instructor’s revised prompt unchanged. Give students ten uninterrupted minutes to develop a position and respond to its strongest objection. Save the responses for the closing reflection.
[Sources]
Duhigg and Kocieniewski, NYT, April 28, 2012

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Discuss your opening arguments
text:
Discuss your opening arguments

What is your strongest reason for or against Apple minimizing its taxes?


Listen to someone who disagrees. What concern does their argument raise for your position?


Class discussion


Timing: 13–16 minutes.
Take one argument on each side and one response. Record the competing claims about shareholders, public services, jobs, and responsibility. Keep the board visible as the mechanisms and social consequences develop.
[Sources]
Duhigg and Kocieniewski, NYT, April 28, 2012, supplied PDF pp. 11–13.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Apple put investment income in Nevada
text:
Apple put investment income in Nevada




David Calvert / NYT, 2012 · Syndicated report.


The 2012 arrangement
Apple’s subsidiary Braeburn Capital invested Apple’s cash.
Locating it in Nevada sheltered some investment income from California tax.
Corporate tax rates in 2012: California 8.84%; Nevada 0%.


This mechanism concerns state revenue. Apple’s overseas arrangements involve separate national tax systems.


Timing: 16–19 minutes.
Explain that the income here is interest and investment returns. A subsidiary is a company owned by another company. Keep the mechanism and rates anchored to the 2012 reporting; the article gives no estimate of this arrangement’s effect on De Anza’s budget.
[Sources]
Duhigg and Kocieniewski, NYT, April 28, 2012, supplied PDF pp. 1–2, 4–5.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: A factory and a tax home give countries a claim to profit
text:
A factory and a tax home give countries a claim to profit
One company has its tax home in Germany, a factory branch in Poland, and customers in France.


Illustration of traditional treaty rules. OECD Model Tax Convention, Articles 7 and 23


Tax residence is the company’s legal home for tax purposes, often based on where it is registered or headquartered.


Timing: 19–23 minutes.
Walk through the same legal company in all three places. Explain tax home as tax residence, which is set by legal rules, rather than a choice of address. Assume a taxable factory branch in Poland and no taxable business presence in France; this illustrates the traditional framework, rather than a finding about a particular bilateral treaty. Explain that home-country credits or exemptions prevent double taxation. Place the League of Nations origins after World War I in this oral background.
[Sources]
OECD Model Tax Convention, Articles 7 and 23; Djankov, PIIE (2021)

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: MNCs Taxed Where Production Occurs
text:
MNCs Taxed Where Production Occurs


Original diagram excerpt: Djankov, PIIE (2021), figure 1.


Country E is the customer market in this simplified model. Assume sales there create no taxable business presence.


Timing: 23–26 minutes.
Trace the production chain from Country B through Country D. Identify headquarters in Country A and the customer market in Country E. Explain that the figure abstracts from local taxable distribution operations in Country E: an actual local subsidiary or branch may owe local profit tax. The home-country treatment includes the double-tax relief just introduced.
[Sources]
Djankov, PIIE (2021); OECD Model Tax Convention, Articles 7 and 23

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: 1. Transfer pricing for physical products
text:
1. Transfer pricing for physical products
A transfer price is a price between related companies.


Original diagram excerpt: Djankov, PIIE (2021), figure 2a.


Low-tax Country D buys cheaply from Country C and sells at a high price to Country E.


Timing: 26–29 minutes.
Trace both product sales in Djankov panel a. High-tax Country C sells cheaply to low-tax Country D; Country D then sells at a high price to the distributor in Country E. Both choices leave more profit in Country D. The next slide simplifies the chain: it omits Country E and lets the Country D subsidiary sell directly to the final customer. State that the arrows show products moving, while payments move back to the sellers. Transfer pricing is a broad set of rules that also applies to related-company royalties; teach the physical-product and IP-license channels as separate examples.
[Sources]
Djankov, PIIE (2021); OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines (2022), chapters I and VI

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Internal prices affect MNC tax bills
text:
Internal prices affect MNC tax bills





Internal price: $80
Internal price: $70




Country C subsidiary profit, taxed at 30%
$20
$10


Country D subsidiary profit, taxed at 10%
$20
$30


Total tax
$6 + $2 = $8
$3 + $3 = $6




Simplified example: the Country D subsidiary sells directly to the customer. Production cost and customer price stay fixed. Other costs and taxes are omitted.


The multinational still earns $40 before tax. Moving $10 of profit to the 10% country saves $2 in tax.


Timing: 29–36 minutes.
Explain that one parent owns both subsidiaries. The Country C subsidiary operates the assembly plant; the Country D subsidiary sells to the independent customer. The preceding Djankov figure includes a separate Country E distributor, which this simplified example omits. Keep production cost at $60 and the final sale at $100. Work through the $80 column first: Country C earns $80 minus $60; Country D earns $100 minus $80. Then ask students to calculate profits at $70 and explain the tax difference. The internal payment cancels in the multinational’s total profit; the $10 transferred between countries saves $2 because the tax rates differ by 20 percentage points. The next slides introduce intangible assets and the separate royalty mechanism. Return to the acceptable-price rules after both examples.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Intangibles can earn income through royalties
text:
Intangibles can earn income through royalties


Proprietary data, patents, software, and brands are intangibles: valuable assets without a physical form.
A royalty is a fee for permission to use them.
Unique data or intellectual property (IP) may have no comparable market transaction.



DeusXFlorida, 2008 · Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.



OECD, hard-to-value intangibles guidance (2018)


Without a reliable market price, royalties are harder to challenge and easier to use for shifting profit.


Timing: 36–39 minutes.
Move from charging for a physical product to charging for permission to use an intangible asset. Introduce the royalty before the next Djankov diagram. Define intellectual property as legally protected creations such as patents, copyrighted software, and trademarks. Explain that a unique dataset or patented technology may have no comparable transaction between independent firms: price then depends heavily on uncertain forecasts of future earnings. This valuation uncertainty gives firms more room to justify charges that shift profit. Tax agencies still use forecasts, valuation models, and profit-split methods to test prices; some intangible licenses have reliable comparables. Use the photograph to illustrate brand value without attributing a tax arrangement to Coca-Cola.
[Sources]
OECD, hard-to-value intangibles guidance (2018); NYT, supplied PDF pp. 9–10.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: 2. Royalties shift profit toward the IP owner
text:
2. Royalties shift profit toward the IP owner
The company in Country D pays the IP owner in Country C for permission to use its IP.


Original diagram excerpt: Djankov, PIIE (2021), figure 2b. The purple arrow shows the IP input; payment goes the other way.


A higher royalty raises costs in high-tax Country D and income in low-tax Country C.


Timing: 39–42 minutes.
Identify the countries afresh: Djankov reverses their tax rates between panels. In panel b, Country C is the low-tax IP owner and Country D is the high-tax operating company. Follow the purple arrow as the intangible input or licensed rights, then trace the royalty payment back from Country D to Country C. The royalty is an expense for the user and income for the owner. Holding the licensed rights and all other costs fixed, a higher deductible royalty moves profit toward the low-tax owner. Djankov discusses both sale and licensing of intangible assets; this class focuses on royalties for licensed rights. Transfer-pricing rules apply to these fees too. Ownership alone cannot justify any fee; actual development work, assets, and risk control matter. The following digital-sales slide raises the separate question of taxing sales without local presence; the enforcement slide then returns to legal limits on product prices and royalties.
[Sources]
Djankov, PIIE (2021), figure 2b and intangible-products discussion; OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines (2022), chapter VI.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: An online seller can reach customers without a local office
text:
An online seller can reach customers without a local office




Helpameout, 2012 · Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.


Consider a streaming company
It sells subscriptions in Country E.
Traditional rules can leave Country E unable to tax its business profit.


Should Country E be able to tax some of the profit earned from its customers? Why?


Timing: 42–45 minutes.
Ask for a reason grounded in the customer relationship and a reason grounded in where the business operates. Treat the hypothetical as having no taxable local presence. Link the example to the reading’s account of downloads sold through Luxembourg. Explain that a business can grow its customer base without expanding its physical presence in each market.
[Sources]

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: The IRS and Irish Revenue enforce transfer-pricing rules
text:
The IRS and Irish Revenue enforce transfer-pricing rules


Who checks the tax return?
U.S. Internal Revenue Service (IRS): profits taxable in the United States.
Irish Revenue: profits taxable in Ireland.
Both can challenge internal product prices and royalties.

Irish enforcement

€824m


from 55 completed transfer-pricing cases over the ten years to 2025



Irish Revenue, Annual Report 2025, p. 56. Reported yield includes €246m in interest and penalties.IRS, transfer pricing.


Arm’s-length pricing: product prices and royalties should reflect terms independent companies would agree to.


Timing: 45–47 minutes.
Identify Irish Revenue as Ireland’s national tax agency. Each agency enforces the rules governing the profits taxable in its country: if a U.S. factory sells too cheaply to a related Irish buyer, the IRS can challenge the resulting understatement of U.S. income. Define the arm’s-length principle as pricing related-company transactions as independent parties would under comparable conditions. Return to both mechanisms: product charges and IP-license fees. Explain that auditors inspect comparable transactions, contracts, and each company’s work; the agencies can reach different conclusions and resolve disputes through treaty procedures. The €824 million is Revenue’s reported yield from completed transfer-pricing interventions over ten years, including interest and penalties, rather than a one-year figure or an Apple-specific result.
[Sources]
IRS, transfer pricing and Section 482; Irish Revenue, Annual Report 2025, p. 56; OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines (2022), chapter I.

section: The EU required Ireland to recover Apple’s tax benefits
text:
The EU required Ireland to recover Apple’s tax benefits


2016: European Commission
Found that Ireland’s tax rulings gave Apple an illegal advantage over other companies.
Ordered Ireland to recover the tax benefits, plus interest.

2024: EU Court of Justice
Upheld the Commission’s decision after years of appeals.

€13bn


Approximate tax benefits to recover, before interest



EU Court of Justice, September 10, 2024. Case concerned Irish tax rulings issued in 1991 and 2007.


Ireland appealed alongside Apple. The EU enforced rules against selective tax advantages granted by a member state.


Timing: 53–55 minutes.
Begin the response section with a concrete enforcement action. The European Commission used existing EU state-aid rules to challenge selective advantages granted through Irish tax rulings. Ireland and Apple challenged the decision; the General Court annulled it in 2020, and the Court of Justice reversed that judgment in 2024 and upheld recovery. Distinguish this proceeding from a routine transfer-pricing audit by Irish Revenue. It illustrates both enforcement and disagreement between national and European authorities. The next slide introduces the 2020 OECD proposal, moving from enforcement under existing EU law to negotiating broader international rules. Avoid inferring the motivation for Ireland’s appeal from aggregate tax receipts.
[Sources]
EU Court of Justice, September 10, 2024.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: The 2021 OECD/G20 agreement proposed two reforms
text:
The 2021 OECD/G20 agreement proposed two reforms


Where companies pay
Pillar One: give customer countries a share of the largest, most profitable multinationals’ profits to tax.
This addresses sales in countries where the seller has little physical presence.

How much companies pay
Pillar Two: set a 15% minimum tax for large multinationals covered by the rules.
This reduces the reward for reporting profit in low-tax countries.


OECD, proposed profit-allocation convention; OECD, global minimum tax.


Governments agreed on the goals in 2021. Each part required further legal steps to take effect. In the U.S., Congressional approval was needed, but did not occur.


Timing: 56–58 minutes.
Connect Pillar One’s Amount A proposal to the earlier streaming-company example: it would allocate a share of profit to customer countries despite limited physical presence. Connect Pillar Two to the transfer-price and royalty examples: a minimum rate reduces the benefit from shifting profit. Explain that agreement on the plan did not enact both parts. The next slide explains the minimum-tax mechanism; the subsequent newspaper headline introduces the political reversal and current outcomes. The profit-allocation convention remains stalled, while many countries began implementing the minimum-tax rules in 2024.
[Sources]
OECD sources linked on the slide.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: U.S. withdrawal narrowed the global tax agreement
text:
U.S. withdrawal narrowed the global tax agreement


The Guardian · January 6, 2026. Headline excerpt.


The profit-allocation treaty is stalled. The minimum tax continues with a U.S. exception.


Timing: 60–63 minutes.
Use the authentic newspaper headline to introduce the political reversal. Explain that the January 20, 2025 presidential memorandum rejected the prior U.S. commitments absent congressional adoption; Congress had not enacted the OECD deal. Distinguish the two outcomes: Pillar One’s Amount A profit-allocation convention remains unopened for signature, while Pillar Two minimum-tax rules have operated in many countries since 2024. The January 2026 side-by-side agreement protects qualifying U.S.-headed multinationals from the income-inclusion and undertaxed-profits rules of other countries; domestic top-up taxes on their local subsidiaries continue to apply. Read the headline alongside that qualification and refer back to the preceding $12 plus $3 example. Close the section by explaining that national interests limit the reach of international tax cooperation. The industry exercise then asks students to identify the profit-shifting incentives these policies address.
[Sources]
The headline is a direct browser capture of the linked Guardian article, limited to its headline text. The technical distinctions rely on OECD, January 2026 side-by-side package, section 5.1, paragraph 7; OECD, Amount A convention status; the White House memorandum and Treasury announcement linked above. Status checked September 12, 2026, including the OECD’s latest implementation guidance.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Calculate the tax bill for a product transaction
text:
Calculate the tax bill for a product transaction
One parent owns a Country C subsidiary with an assembly plant and a Country D selling subsidiary. This example involves a physical product. There are no other costs or taxes.


Country C subsidiary
Its assembly plant makes one product for $50.
Pays 30% tax on its profit.

Country D subsidiary
Buys the product from Country C and sells it to a customer for $120.
Pays 10% tax on its profit.


Compare internal prices of $80 and $100. Which price gives the multinational a lower tax bill, and why?


Timing: 63–73 minutes.
Leave this slide on screen for the full calculation. Allow roughly six minutes for the comparison and four for checking and writing an explanation. Visit teams to check that Country C’s sales revenue is Country D’s purchase cost. Keep the complete private solution in the instructor activity key.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Apply the royalty mechanism to your industry
text:
Apply the royalty mechanism to your industry

Turn to the people near you. Each person names their industry and one kind of valuable IP it uses, such as software, a patent, or a brand. It’s fine if some of you have the same industry. Pick one example. Imagine a company in a low-tax country owns that IP and charges a related operating company a royalty to use it. What is the operating company paying for? If the royalty rises, where does reported profit go up, and where does it go down?


Timing: 73–77 minutes.
This exercise follows the separate royalty mechanism. Ask teams to apply their industry knowledge to an IP license, while inventing all corporate and tax details. Require a high-tax payer, a low-tax IP owner, and a payment arrow from user to owner. The higher royalty reduces the payer’s profit and raises the recipient’s profit, holding other facts fixed.
